labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body: ### What issue are you seeing? The app-server thread/list API currently treats an omitted/null modelProviders field as an implicit filter for the currently configured model provider. If a third party app doesn't include the modelProviders field, then not all threads are shown. This issue is especially annoying when trying to continue a thread with a different model provider, as many apps, including Codex Desktop, don't see the thread with the new model provider. While this issue could be fixed both on the desktop and app server side, I think this is more of an app server issue than a desktop one, since an omitted filter shouldn't be filtering by default. ### What steps can reproduce the bug? ## App server 1. Create local threads under at least two model providers, for example openai and lcpp. 2. Configure Codex so the active provider is one of them, for example: ```toml model_provider = "lcpp" [model_providers.lcpp] name = "Llama.cpp" base_url = "http://localhost:8080/v1" wire_api = "responses" ``` 3. Call app-server thread/list with modelProviders omitted or set to null. 4. Observe that only threads for the active provider are returned. 5. Call thread/list again with: ``` { "modelProviders": [] } ``` 6. Observe that threads from all providers are returned. ## Desktop 1. Open Codex with default OpenAI config 2. Send message in a folder 3. Quit Codex Desktop 4. Change config to use another model and provider 5. Reopen Codex 6. See that threads previously used are missing, only threads that used that provider previously are visible. This is also inconsistent with the CLI since the CLI still lists threads that were started with other model providers. Here is a screenshot with my OpenAI login, using the default OpenAI provider and model=gpt-5.5 in the config: After quitting Codex, changing my config to the following, this is what I see: ``` model_provider = "lcpp" model = "qwen3.6-27b-mtp" ``` ### What is the expected behavior? Current behavior appears to be: - modelProviders: ["openai"] returns only openai threads. - modelProviders: [] returns all providers. - modelProviders: null / omitted returns only threads matching the current configured provider. What it should be: - modelProviders: ["lcpp"] means only lcpp. - modelProviders: [] means all providers. - modelProviders: null / omitted means also all providers. On the desktop side, I expect that my threads will still show up after switching providers. ### Additional information I pointed Codex to the desktop app.asar, and it confirmed that the desktop app currently sends listAllThreads({ modelProviders: null }) which is why threads go missing in the desktop app after switching model providers. If the app server is behaving as intended and you would rather fix it on the desktop app side, then switch model providers to be modelProviders: [] and it will include all threads from all model providers. Again this is inconsistent with the CLI since in the CLI you can resume across different model providers. This issue is the root cause of Relevant code is here in main: https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3da89d4831251b704ac40d1357d26ad518abaf1d/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs#L3457 I also had drafted a fix but can't open a PR since I don't have permission: https://github.com/joshrad-dev/codex/tree/fix-thread-list-null-model-provider. This code is the cause and fix for the following issues: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/20184 https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/20004 https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/19088 After getting Codex to patch the ASAR to use [] instead of null for the modelProviders send, I'm now able to see all my threads across providers.

issues.title: Windows: unbounded per-untracked-file Git fan-out; 24 GiB status working set after bulk intent-to-add workaround

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body:
## Summary

Codex on native Windows can fan out one `git diff --binary --no-index` process per visible untracked path during `gitDiffToRemote`. Large local research/output trees turn this into a severe process and memory risk.

An independent local diagnostic established the per-file fan-out on a four-file disposable fixture. A custom mitigation subsequently added untracked files as intent-to-add entries. That avoided the per-file fan-out, but incorrectly included a large generated archive tree. This made full status checks extremely expensive. This report explicitly distinguishes the product behavior from that local mitigation mistake.

## Environment

- Windows 11 Business, x64, version 10.0.26200.
- Dell Precision 5690, approximately 32 GB installed RAM / 31.46 GiB usable.
- Desktop app checker: installedVersion 26.1007.21434, build 13901, prod.
- Current MSIX package: OpenAI.Codex 26.1007.2314.0. Package and app version identifiers are different.
- Bundled CLI checked on October 13: codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.17.2.
- Git for Windows 2.54.0.1.
- Native local workspace, not WSL. Mobile Remote is regularly used.
- Multiple concurrent tasks. No crash-inducing stress test was run.

## Directly verified observations

### 1. Per-file subprocess fan-out

A bounded, isolated four-untracked-file fixture was queried through the local app-server's `gitDiffToRemote`:

| Fixture | Per-file --no-index Git commands | Returned diff bytes |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Four ordinary untracked text files | 4 | 608 |
| Same files registered as intent-to-add | 0 | 608 |

Before the local workaround, the affected real workspaces had 24,217 and 2,614 untracked paths respectively. Those counts are potential workload size; they are not claimed to be a simultaneous process census.

### 2. Very large resident memory in full Git status

On October 13 a live read-only command with this shape was recorded at **24.12 GiB working set**:

```text
git status --renames --porcelain=v1 -z --untracked-files=normal
```

An earlier private-memory measurement for that process was approximately **0.207 GiB**. Resident memory and private commit are not interchangeable. Stopping that read-only status was followed by physical RAM utilization returning to approximately 45.3%.

### 3. Local workaround aggravated the status workload — corrected

Our custom normalizer had automatically registered roughly 70,700 files in a generated research/archive tree as intent-to-add. The tree had approximately 94.75 GiB **logical** file contents, including compressed/hardlinked historical copies. This is not 94.75 GiB newly created by Git, and is not its exclusive physical storage.

On October 13 at approximately 22:56 America/Toronto, we:
- added local exclusion rules for only these generated archive families;
- removed **70,708 intent-to-add entries** through a private-index transaction;
- verified every unrelated index entry and the prepared/staged raw diff were unchanged;
- left all working files untouched;
- prevented the normalizer from enrolling those archive families again.

The primary index went from **74,554 to 3,846 entries**. The same status command then completed successfully in **0.104 seconds**, with 19,417 output bytes and no stderr. The timing supports the generated-index workload as a major contributor on this machine. It does not prove that every historical failure had this cause.

### 4. Latest application closure was a custom safety action

October 13, America/Toronto (UTC-4):
- 22:17:13: Windows Application Error 1000 for git.exe, exception 0xc0000005.
- 22:18:16: a task started a broad shell Git status in the large primary workspace.
- 22:18:57: our independent guard recorded physical RAM at **95.98%**.
- 22:18:59: that guard intentionally closed the desktop/backends.
- 22:20:00: the guard reopened the desktop.
- The laptop's last boot remained 19:26:17; no laptop reboot occurred during this incident.

The latest desktop closure is therefore **not being reported as an unexplained native desktop crash**. The access violation, later shell status and missing historical resident-memory samples do not establish a complete causal chain. The guard originally covered GUI status but missed shell status; that gap has now also been corrected.

## Expected behavior / requested engineering changes

- Bound concurrent Git subprocesses globally and per repository in `gitDiffToRemote`, including the untracked-file path.
- Stream or cap path enumeration and diff output instead of eagerly scheduling a process for every untracked file.
- Coalesce repeated automatic scans and apply a circuit breaker/backoff after resource errors, cancellation or timeout.
- Correctly terminate and reap complete Git process trees on Windows.
- Allow supported disabling of expensive automatic Git review/status activity, including Remote-triggered work, without disabling agent execution or ordinary messages.
- Add diagnostics that distinguish resident mapped pages from private commit and identify the actual scan caller.
- Large generated research trees should cause a bounded unavailable/partial review result, never jeopardize the user's running tasks or OS.

## Related reports

- #41982: Remote chat opening and Windows Git/OOM incidents.
- #41091: composer_content/watch-repo full-status retries.
- #45172: Windows root-first cancellation race.
- #53645: thousands of app-server Git children in the current desktop build.

This report adds a bounded per-untracked-file reproduction, a directly observed 24.12 GiB status working set, and the measured effect of removing a mistakenly created bulk intent-to-add workload. It does not assert that all related reports share one proven root cause.

## Privacy

Text-only technical report. No raw logs, conversation exports, account identifiers, credentials, repository URLs, private project names, user-specific paths, or project contents are included.

Observed September 30, 2026, with a post-update retest on October 1, 2026. Cached first-party codex-app-tools version: 0.1.5. Delegated testing used GPT-6.1 Sol with Medium reasoning.

The dot has cloud_threads tools, but lookup of the verified local thread returns “thread not found.” Exact callable checks for mcp__codex_app__list_threads, mcp__codex_app__read_thread, and mcp__codex_app__send_message_to_thread return undefined. ### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Keep the Windows PC connected with Codex Desktop open and an existing local conversation available.
2. Ask dot to communicate with that specific existing local conversation. Creating and running a delegated local task on the PC succeeds, but it is a separate conversation.
3. Inspect dot’s available tools and attempt the supported existing-thread lookup.
4. Observe the local-thread lookup returning “thread not found” and the exact native list/read/send methods remaining unavailable.

On October 1, after the user installed a pending update and restarted Codex, the PC remained connected and authorized, but lookup still failed and the native methods remained absent in both the parent and helper. A new installed executable was found, reporting CLI 0.159.2. The permitted package query returned no result, so the updated Desktop package version was not verified. No new message was sent to the target conversation in this retest.

### What is the expected behavior?

dot should be able to read and communicate with an explicitly authorized existing local conversation, preserving its identity and history, or clearly explain the supported availability boundary and recovery route.

### Additional tested evidence

- A prior permitted provider probe initialized successfully, then tools/list failed with JSON-RPC -32603 and “connect EPERM” on the Desktop named pipe. The opaque pipe identifier is omitted. That denied route was stopped; no tools/call followed.
- Installed CLI default-context diagnostics reported “Could not find home directory” and “failed to resolve CODEX_HOME.” Two specifically approved outside-sandbox diagnostics resolved home/configuration and showed the provider reachable. app-server daemon version still failed to connect to the default control socket with Windows OS error 10050. This does not establish a general internet outage.
- A separate supported queue/history test verified one message inserted into the intended existing conversation. Its response was interrupted when the test connection closed; a later continuation encountered an active-writer conflict. Queue acceptance/history insertion is not native sender attribution or verified two-way communication. No acknowledgment or working repair was verified.

### Requested investigation

Please diagnose native existing-thread capability provisioning for this task origin. Is this an intended availability boundary, a host registration/discovery failure, or a missing catalog projection? These are hypotheses, not established causes. Please identify a supported recovery that preserves existing conversations and permissions.

This report contains technical version data and redacted error text only. No raw logs, transcripts, screenshots, credentials, private file contents, or identifying thread/account/device paths are attached.

### Relevant public references

$200

### What issue are you seeing?

OAuth login to the Meta Ads MCP server fails after browser authorization.

Server: https://mcp.facebook.com/ads
Codex CLI: 0.162.0-alpha.17.2
Platform: Windows

With a pre-registered OAuth client, the browser callback displays:
Authentication complete. You may close this window.

However, the CLI exits with:
Error: failed to handle OAuth callback
Caused by:
OAuth token exchange failed: missing field `access_token` at line 1 column 191

A fresh configuration using automatic client registration fails with:
invalid_client_metadata: Dynamic registration is not available for this client.

RUST_LOG=debug and RUST_LOG=trace,codex_core=trace did not expose the token endpoint HTTP status or response body. Only the summarized error was captured.

Related report: #38944 describes a related Meta registration failure, but does not establish the cause of this token exchange error.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Configure https://mcp.facebook.com/ads as a Streamable HTTP MCP server, with a pre-registered OAuth client ID and the exact callback URI registered with the provider.

Configuration structure (replace placeholders with valid registered values):

[mcp_servers.meta_ads]
url = "https://mcp.facebook.com/ads"

[mcp_servers.meta_ads.oauth]
client_id = "<REGISTERED_CLIENT_ID>"
callback_url = "<REGISTERED_CALLBACK_URL>"
callback_port = 5555

2. Run:
codex mcp login meta_ads

3. Complete authorization on Facebook.

4. Observe that the callback page displays "Authentication complete", while the CLI exits with the missing access_token error.

5. Repeat with RUST_LOG=trace,codex_core=trace and log_dir configured. The same failure occurs without the original token endpoint response being logged.

Separate automatic-registration test:
codex mcp add meta_ads_novo --url https://mcp.facebook.com/ads

This fails with:
invalid_client_metadata: Dynamic registration is not available for this client.

### What is the expected behavior?

With a valid pre-registered OAuth client and registered callback, Codex should complete the token exchange and save the credentials.

If the provider rejects the exchange, Codex should display the HTTP status and a sanitized provider error message, rather than only reporting a missing access_token field.

The callback page should distinguish receipt of the authorization code from successful completion of authentication.

### Additional information

The issue occurs during MCP authentication, before model usage.

Both the existing configuration with a pre-registered client and a fresh configuration using automatic registration were tested. They failed at different stages.

The underlying token endpoint response remains unknown, so the cause of the token exchange failure has not been established.

OpenAI support recommended filing this issue after debug and trace logging did not expose the original response. A redacted codex doctor report is included above.

No access tokens, client secrets, authorization codes, or full callback URLs are included in this report.

Additional OAuth configuration used:

client_id: 1431989845511004
redirect_uri: http://localhost:5555/callback/p3oJPar44nR2
Codex CLI: 0.162.0-alpha.17.2
MCP server: https://mcp.facebook.com/ads

Captured error:
OAuth token exchange failed: missing field `access_token` at line 1 column 191

Debug and trace logging did not expose the token endpoint HTTP status or response body.

issues.body: ### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)? 26.730.61639 ### What subscription do you have? Pro ### What platform is your computer? Windows for the App, Ubuntu 24.04 and Ubuntu 26.04 for CLI ### What issue are you seeing? Description I use the Codex desktop app on Windows with multiple SSH connections to Linux systems running Codex CLI. These SSH connections are configured directly inside the Windows Codex app under: Settings → Connections → SSH All configured SSH connections show Connected, and I have several active SSH-backed projects that I regularly open and use from the Windows Codex app without any problems. However, when I connect to that same Windows computer using Remote in the Android mobile app, only direct/local chats appear. None of the active projects associated with the Windows app’s SSH connections are displayed. These are not arbitrary SSH sessions launched manually in PowerShell. They are established SSH connections recognized by the Codex desktop app, and the projects are already visible and functional in the desktop app. Environment Host: Codex desktop app on Windows Client: ChatGPT/Codex app on Android Both devices signed into the same account Control this PC enabled on Windows Mobile device successfully paired with the Windows computer Multiple SSH connections configured in the Windows Codex app All SSH connections show Connected Multiple active SSH-backed projects are visible and usable in the desktop app Impact This prevents me from monitoring or continuing my active Linux development projects from mobile, even though: The Windows computer is online and paired successfully. The SSH connections are active. The projects work normally in the Windows desktop app. Direct chats from that same Windows host appear correctly on mobile. The current behavior makes Remote useful only for direct Windows chats and breaks continuity for users whose primary Codex workflow uses the desktop app’s SSH connections. ### What steps can reproduce the bug? Steps to reproduce Open the Codex desktop app on Windows. Go to Settings → Connections → SSH. Confirm that the configured Linux SSH hosts show Connected. Open and use one or more projects associated with those SSH connections. Enable Control this PC and pair the Android mobile app with the Windows computer. Open Remote on the Android device. Select the paired Windows computer. Review the available chats and projects. ### What is the expected behavior? Actual result Only direct/local Codex chats from the Windows computer are displayed. The active projects associated with the Windows app’s connected SSH environments do not appear in the mobile Remote interface. Expected result The mobile Remote interface should display the active SSH-backed projects and chats that are already recognized, connected, and usable through the paired Windows Codex desktop app. At minimum, the mobile app should allow existing SSH-backed project conversations to be opened and monitored in the same way as direct/local Codex chats. ### Additional information Additional clarification This report is not asking the mobile app to discover arbitrary standalone Codex CLI sessions. The missing projects are already listed as active projects inside the Windows Codex desktop app and are associated with SSH connections that the app reports as connected. Screenshots I can provide two screenshots: Connections screen: Shows multiple SSH connections with a Connected status. Projects screen: Shows multiple active projects assigned to those SSH hosts. The individual project and server names have been redacted for privacy.

issues.title: Daemon bootstrap reports success while its updater exits with SUN_LEN under a deep CODEX_HOME (Linux)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body:
## Behaviour

On Linux with codex-cli 0.160.0, `app-server daemon bootstrap` successfully starts the managed app-server and records a daemon-updater PID, but the updater immediately exits when its Unix socket path exceeds the platform address limit. Its stderr contains `Error: path must be shorter than SUN_LEN`, and `daemon-updater.sock` never appears. The serving daemon survives, so an immediate PID-file check can incorrectly suggest that auto-update is working.

Observed in a private HOME under a pytest directory on 2026-10-03. No production daemon was stopped or restarted. The fixture's updater socket was longer than Linux's 108-byte Unix-address field. A short private HOME under disk TMPDIR produces a 99-byte updater address and is the proposed fixture workaround.

## Source

The updater binds its manual-update listener directly to `manual_update_socket_path()` in [update_loop.rs:118–128](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/app-server-daemon/src/update_loop.rs#L118).

That path is the updater PID-file path with a `.sock` extension, with no short-address mapping, in [lib.rs:993–995](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/app-server-daemon/src/lib.rs#L993).

The existing [deep control-socket path report](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/27765) describes daemon-client control addresses in 0.137/0.139 on macOS. This reproduction concerns the updater's separate socket in 0.160.0 on Linux; the app-server control socket itself works through its existing long-path fallback.

## Reproduction

1. Create a private HOME on disk with a long absolute path. Set `CODEX_HOME` to its `.codex` directory. Choose the length so `$CODEX_HOME/app-server-daemon/daemon-updater.sock` exceeds 108 bytes.
2. Copy the installed 0.160.0 app-server release into that private home's `packages/app-server-daemon/releases/0.160.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, create `current` pointing at that release, and write that release name without a newline to `auto-update-version`. Never share writable package files or lifecycle state with the real HOME.
3. In the private `app-server-daemon/settings.json`, enable automatic updates and set shutdown grace to zero. Use a private config and no credentials.
4. Run the private binary with HOME, CODEX_HOME and TMPDIR explicitly set to private paths:

   ```sh
   "$private_codex" app-server daemon bootstrap
   ```

5. After bootstrap succeeds, read `app-server-daemon/daemon-updater.pid`, inspect that process, the updater socket, and `daemon-updater.stderr.log`.

Observed: the updater exits, the socket is absent, and stderr reports SUN_LEN; the daemon accepts a turn. Shortening only the private HOME makes the updater address fit. Stop only the private daemon and updater when finished.

## Expected

The updater should use a private short-address mapping for long paths, consistently with app-server control sockets. Bootstrap should not report a working updater merely because its PID record was published before startup failed. A regression should verify the updater stays alive and serves its socket after bootstrap with a long CODEX_HOME.

Environment: codex-cli 0.160.0 (npm, linux-x64 musl), Ubuntu, managed app-server daemon.

issues.title: [macOS][Remote SSH] Follow-up submission fails with no-client-found after thread owner changes

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

ChatGPT/Codex macOS desktop app `26.928.31416`, build `12553` (read from the installed bundle's Info.plist).

Remote Codex CLI: `0.159.0`.

### What subscription do you have?

Signed in with ChatGPT. Subscription tier not included in this report.

### What platform is your computer?

- Local: macOS `27.0.1`, Apple Silicon / `arm64`.
- Remote: Linux `6.8.0-136-generic`, `x86_64`, running in a Docker container and accessed through the desktop app's Remote SSH connection.

### What issue are you seeing?

Sending a follow-up message to an existing Remote SSH conversation repeatedly fails immediately with `no-client-found`. The affected conversation is displayed in another desktop window and is logged as a `follower` of a different client. The remote conversation can still be read successfully.

The failure was observed repeatedly on 2026-10-01, including at `05:53:45`, `05:53:48`, `05:57:07`, `05:57:45`, and `06:00:46` UTC. Reopening the affected conversation through the desktop app's navigation tool did not resolve it; the user retried and confirmed the same error.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence (the exact trigger for the stale ownership state is not yet isolated):

1. Connect the macOS desktop app to a Linux Remote SSH host and open an existing conversation.
2. Have multiple desktop windows involved with that conversation. Logs show the affected window following an owner in another client.
3. Ownership changes to another client while the affected window remains a follower.
4. Send a follow-up from the affected window.
5. The composer fails with `no-client-found` instead of starting the next turn.
6. Navigate back to the same conversation and retry: the same error persists in the observed session.

Closing the secondary window and retrying from the original window has been proposed, but its result has not yet been verified. A full desktop restart has not been tested. This report does not claim deterministic reproduction from a clean launch.

### What is the expected behavior?

A live follower window should submit the message through the current owner, or recover/reacquire ownership if that client has disappeared. The user should be able to continue an otherwise readable remote conversation without an opaque `no-client-found` error.

### Additional information

Sanitized desktop log excerpts below. Thread/client identifiers and the workspace path are replaced with placeholders; repeated placeholders retain their relationships.

```text
2026-10-01T05:40:17.053Z info [electron-message-handler] thread_stream_role_changed
  conversationId=<thread>
  ownerClientId=<owner-B> previousOwnerClientId=<owner-A>
  previousRole=follower role=follower
  rendererWebContentsId=6 rendererWindowId=4
  rendererWindowAppearance=primary
  rendererWindowFocused=false rendererWindowVisible=true

2026-10-01T06:00:46.403Z error [electron-message-handler] [Composer] submit failed
  cwd=<remote-workspace>
  errorMessage=no-client-found errorName=Error
  followUp=local mode=local
  rendererWebContentsId=6 rendererWindowId=4
  rendererWindowAppearance=primary
  rendererWindowFocused=true rendererWindowVisible=true
  errorStack="Error: no-client-found
    at e.evaluateImpl (app://-/assets/app-shared-44edd7bfa69c.js:419:44787)
    at e.evaluateWithDepth (app://-/assets/app-shared-44edd7bfa69c.js:419:42515)
    at e.evaluate (app://-/assets/app-shared-44edd7bfa69c.js:419:42398)
    at HBt.readLoop (app://-/assets/app-shared-44edd7bfa69c.js:419:59251)"
```

Isolation performed during the failure:

- Direct SSH commands to the remote host succeeded in approximately 0.7 seconds.
- The dedicated remote proxy was running and the remote CLI reported that it was signed in with ChatGPT.
- Remote app-server processes were present.
- The desktop connection remained connected; account/history requests and reading the affected conversation succeeded. These checks establish that remote reads worked, not that a new model turn could start.

Read-only inspection of the installed desktop JavaScript correlated this error with the IPC request path: request client lookup fails and returns `no-client-found`; follower turn submission uses forwarding to the owner. This is consistent with stale/unavailable owner routing, but it is a hypothesis rather than a proven root cause.

Potential areas to investigate: owner liveness validation on follow-up submission, cleanup/re-election after a client or renderer disappears, and fallback recovery when owner forwarding returns `no-client-found`.

Related ownership-discovery report: #37397. That issue concerns a five-second local-thread resume timeout; this report concerns immediate follow-up submission failure on a Remote SSH conversation.

Raw logs, session transcripts, host addresses, and credentials are not attached.

issues.title: [macOS Desktop] codex reaches 73.9 GB footprint during memory_stage1 extraction of a 26.3 GB history

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
## Summary
The bundled codex backend repeatedly reaches tens of gigabytes during ordinary ChatGPT desktop use on a 24 GB Mac. New read-only diagnostics identify a running memory_stage1 job for a 26,315,095,941-byte saved history, repeated loads of that same history before three incidents, and stable sampled worker stacks in memory-history serialization and secret redaction. The latest process sample reports a 73.9G physical footprint; its allocation summary is dominated by native malloc regions, much of which is swapped out.

A macOS application-memory warning was followed shortly by a Codex crash. I manually restarted the Mac afterward. The reboot was a recovery action; no automatic reboot, kernel panic, or verified application-crash cause is claimed.

This appears closely related to #53039 and #51233. Please consolidate if appropriate. This adds macOS evidence on the same bundled backend version as #53039, two matching stack captures, a 26.3 GB history, and detailed heap/swap measurements.

The 26.3 GB chat history loaded and functioned normally in the foreground for days without issue; the runaway memory growth only occurs when the background memory_stage1 extraction job attempts to process it.

## Environment
- ChatGPT desktop: 26.1007.30912, build 20156 (installed bundle metadata).
- Bundled backend: codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.17.2 (bundled executable --version).
- Codex Framework: 155.0.8059.40 (running executable paths).
- macOS: 27.0.1, build 26A434; ARM64.
- Hardware identifier: Mac18,5; 24 GB RAM.
- Startup filesystem had approximately 121.5 GiB available during capture.
- Existing profile; no clean-install reproduction performed.
- Relevant configuration, read without changes:
  [features]
  memories = true
  [memories]
  generate_memories = true
  use_memories = true

## Measured timeline
All times below are October 13, 2026, America/Chicago (UTC-05:00).

1. 16:39:37: backend diagnostic log records loading the large history (History A, 26,315,095,941 bytes) alongside another history. A prior support investigation reported a 55.0G footprint for this earlier launch; that prior sample was not remeasured here. This load is now independently verified from the backend log.
2. 19:39:27: the same History A is loaded again. A second history loaded simultaneously reports context_length_exceeded six seconds later. That error belongs to the smaller history and must not be misattributed to History A.
3. 19:47:55: an Activity Monitor sample confirms footprint/peak 71.5G. Its sampled worker remains in serialize_filtered_rollout_response_items -> redact_secrets -> regex search for 2,149 observations. The process Memory column showed 71.47 GB; system swap 65.92 GB; compressed memory 11.79 GB; yellow memory pressure. The visible renderer and ChatGPT parent were approximately 762 MB and 359 MB.
4. A macOS memory warning was followed shortly by a Codex crash, I then manually restarted the Mac. No matching panic or Codex/ChatGPT application crash report was found by a date/name check in the two standard diagnostic-report directories inspected.
5. 19:57:54: the currently sampled backend launches after the reboot.
6. 20:42:12: memory job metadata shows kind=memory_stage1, status=running, started_at=20:42:12, lease_until=21:42:12, finished_at=NULL, retry_remaining=3 for History A. Backend logs show the same history loading at the same second. Another 392,866,603-byte history loads concurrently and fails at 20:42:18 with context_length_exceeded.
7. Around 20:45: Activity Monitor shows the new backend at 43.83 GB, system swap 33.27 GB, and compressed memory 12.06 GB. The largest visible renderer is 596 MB, and ChatGPT parent 339 MB.
8. 20:52:37: a three-second process sample (10 ms sampling interval) reports footprint/peak 73.9G. The relevant worker remains in the same memory-serialization/redaction path for all 265 captured observations.
9. 20:52:41: vmmap -summary also reports footprint/peak 73.9G. A later process-list check confirms the same backend PID is still running; no diagnostic command terminated it.

## Allocation evidence
Selected vmmap values, retaining the tool's reported units:
- Writable regions: total 93.2G; resident 2.7G; swapped out 71.3G; unallocated 19.3G.
- Malloc Large: virtual size 62.8G; resident/dirty 1.6G; swapped 58.3G.
- Malloc Small: virtual size 13.1G; resident/dirty 560.3M; swapped 12.3G.
- Mapped files: 35.2M virtual; 464K resident; no swapped bytes reported.
- Stack: 374.4M virtual; 5.6M resident; 13.5M swapped.
- Total process resident size: approximately 3.1G, despite footprint 73.9G.

The malloc zones dominate the observed footprint; it is not simply a 74 GB mapped file or virtual-address reservation. The zone table separately reports 89.3G bytes allocated. This metric differs from footprint; no claim is made that each value represents the same accounting basis. No allocation-origin heap profile was captured.

## Sampled execution lead
Both independently captured high-footprint processes include:
```text
  codex_memories_write::phase1::job::serialize_filtered_rollout_response_items
  codex_secrets::sanitizer::redact_secrets
  regex_automata search
```

Combined with the exact current memory job/history/load-time match, this strongly points to automatic background memory extraction of oversized stored history. It does not identify the exact allocation stack retaining every byte, prove why the history grew so large, or establish whether redaction itself is responsible for the allocations. The largest history was last modified at 06:28 CDT, hours before the current job. Its contents were not read or uploaded in this investigation; only size and associated job metadata were inspected.

## Observed steps and reproduction status
1. Run ChatGPT desktop 26.1007.30912 with the existing profile and the memory-generation settings listed above. The profile contains a 26,315,095,941-byte saved chat history.
2. Use the app normally. The exact foreground chat/navigation and the event that selected this history for processing have not been established.
3. The backend claims a memory_stage1 job for that history and logs loading it. In the latest occurrence, both timestamps are 20:42:12 CDT.
4. During that occurrence, observe codex reach 43.83 GB in Activity Monitor around 20:45, then a 73.9G footprint in sample/vmmap around 20:52. Both high-footprint stack captures show the history-serialization/redaction path.
5. In an earlier occurrence, a macOS memory warning was followed shortly by a Codex crash, prompting a manual restart. After relaunch, the same history was selected again and the growth recurred.

This is an observed sequence, not a claim that the foreground actions alone deterministically reproduce the problem. The private history has not been replayed in a separate test environment.

## Expected and actual behavior
Expected: background extraction applies a byte/record/memory bound before materializing or serializing a very large history; oversized inputs fail safely or are skipped, and one old chat cannot exhaust the machine. A failed or interrupted job should not repeatedly load the same fatal input without effective safeguards.
Actual: the same 26.3 GB saved history is loaded before repeated runaway episodes, with a currently running extraction job, 71.5G and 73.9G sampled footprints, severe system swap, and a reported memory-warning crash.

## Reproduction status and limitations
- This is an observed existing-profile failure, not a credential-free controlled reproduction.
- No additional large-history load was deliberately triggered. Cloning/replaying the 26.3 GB input would add unnecessary pressure to this already affected machine.
- No configuration, database, history, or application files were changed during diagnosis; local report/evidence files were created. No process was killed.
- A bounded desktop-log inspection also finds background access-denied history reads and ResizeObserver errors. These are secondary observations and do not establish the cause of native backend allocation. The memory-job and stack evidence is stronger.
- Disk activity and swap counts do not quantify NAND wear. A prior macOS codex disk-writes resource diagnostic records approximately 8.59 GB file-backed memory dirtied over roughly 10 hours on October 12; that is neither a swap-write count nor an SSD-health assessment.

## Related reports
- #53039: background extraction of inactive oversized history on Linux, backend 0.162.0-alpha.17.2. Closest version/path comparison; the other report's private input and allocation profile differ.
- #51233: automatic extraction of image-heavy histories and repeated OOM on backend 0.160.0. Similar pipeline and retry concern; this history's image/content composition has not been established.
- #36971: other macOS native heap growth. Older version and different sampled symbols.
- #53178: access-denied background hydration on desktop build 20156. Co-occurrence does not prove a memory-growth cause.

## Nota bene
I'm not a developer. I created a GitHub account to pass this along after my Mac kept throwing this memory error, and used Codex to generate the diagnostics.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1007.2314.0, verified from the currently running Windows package path. About-dialog version was not captured. The affected desktop session records bundled Codex version 0.162.0-alpha.17.2.

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows x64; Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.19045.0. Standalone ChatGPT/Codex desktop app, local Work conversation (session originator: codex_work_desktop).

### What issue are you seeing?

On 2026-10-13, an existing local Work conversation in the Windows desktop app failed on three consecutive attempts after substantial waiting. Two turns ended with a response-stream error; the intervening turn ended with a model-capacity error. Earlier turns in the same conversation had completed successfully.

The affected turns recorded model `gpt-6.1-sol` with reasoning effort `ultra`. The task involved reading local documents, revising analysis and producing structured output files. Progress messages and/or file edits occurred before failure, but the affected turns did not reach a final completion response. The latest inspected failure left the conversation in `systemError` state. This report concerns desktop task execution; it does not establish a cause for any mobile Remote loading problem.

Observed terminal failures (all times JST / Asia/Tokyo, UTC+09:00, 2026-10-13):

| Turn started | Turn failed | Elapsed | Terminal error |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 19:41:40 | 19:59:39 | 17m 59s | stream disconnected before completion |
| 20:39:53 | 20:51:20 | 11m 27s | Selected model is at capacity |
| 20:51:31 | 21:00:48 | 9m 17s | stream disconnected before completion |

Exact error text, with request identifiers redacted:

```text
stream disconnected before completion: An error occurred while processing your request. You can retry your request, or contact us through our help center at help.openai.com if the error persists. Please include the request ID [redacted] in your message.
```

```text
Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.
```

The two stream failures contained distinct request IDs, retained locally for any appropriate private support follow-up. Raw conversations and local source documents are not attached.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed workflow rather than a guaranteed minimal reproduction:
1. Open an established local Work conversation in the standalone Windows desktop app.
2. Use gpt-6.1-sol with ultra reasoning effort.
3. Ask it to read local documents, revise a prior analysis and produce several structured output files. Sanitized task description: continue the existing document-analysis work and complete the revised deliverables.
4. The run produces progress and/or file edits, then fails after a lengthy wait instead of producing its final response.
5. Follow-up/continuation attempts in the same conversation show the sequence recorded above: stream failure, model-capacity failure, then another stream failure.

Earlier successful turns in this conversation were observed, including a document conversion. A later continuation may still be attempted; this report does not claim the conversation is permanently unrecoverable. Model switching, VPN-off testing, a fresh-thread comparison and cross-client testing have not been performed specifically for these failures. Token-limit/context-window usage was not collected for this report.

### What is the expected behavior?

The task should complete reliably or recover and resume safely after an interruption. If the selected model cannot serve the request, the app should surface that promptly and offer a clear recovery path while preserving completed work. A run that has already shown progress should not leave the user waiting for 9–18 minutes and then end without its final response or an actionable explanation.

### Additional information

Evidence comes from read-only inspection of the affected desktop conversation's recorded turn status/errors/timestamps and its recorded model configuration. Elapsed times are recorded turn durations, not a measurement of network timeout thresholds.

Please investigate the repeated failures and the late model-capacity error, including how the app presents interruption/recovery. These observations do not establish whether the cause is service capacity, response transport, the client, context handling, local networking, or multiple independent failures.

The user previously reported using Astrill VPN. The exact VPN route at these failure times was not captured, so VPN causation is unverified.

Possibly related symptom reports: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/52919 and https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/37647. This report adds the October 13 sequence and the gpt-6.1-sol ultra / late-capacity observation; a shared root cause has not been established.

Subscription tier was not collected. Private document contents, file paths, email address, session IDs and raw logs have been omitted.

prs.title: Reuse staged file digests when preparing daemon installs
prs.body:
Reuse staged file digests when preparing daemon installs

## Why

Daemon installation rereads staged files to verify the executable and hash the normalized WinGet package, even though staging already computed their digests.

## What changed

Cache file digests while copying the package and reuse them for the staged executable comparison and final WinGet tree hash. Update cached paths when moving WinGet executables and refresh digests when rewriting manifests.

Continue hashing source packages and existing releases from disk so digest reuse does not bypass content validation.

## Testing

Extend the installation test to corrupt an existing release's `codex-package.json` and verify that reinstalling rejects it while preserving the current selection.

prs.title: Fix daemon updater socket binding and bootstrap readiness on Unix
prs.body:
Fix daemon updater socket binding and bootstrap readiness on Unix

## Why

The updater bound its socket directly beneath `CODEX_HOME`, which can exceed Unix socket path limits. Bootstrap could also report success before the updater's manual-update socket was ready.

issues.title: Body timeout is fixed at 300 s for API-key auth; a long silent tool call is dropped and replayed

labels.name: status/need-triage
labels.description: Issues that need to be triaged by the triage automation.

labels.name: area/core
labels.description: Issues related to User Interface, OS Support, Core Functionality

issues.body:
### What happened?

With `@google/gemini-cli` 0.64.0 in headless mode (`-p`, `--output-format stream-json`), API-key auth and `gemini-4-argon` at `thinkingLevel: HIGH`, a turn in which the model writes one large tool-call argument (for example a whole document passed to `write_file`) can stream nothing for more than 300 seconds. undici then aborts the response with `UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT`. Telemetry records `gemini_cli.api_error` with `exception TypeError: fetch failed sending request` or `terminated`, and the CLI replays the same request from scratch, up to `maxAttempts` (default 10). In our runs, two turns ended with `[API Error: terminated]` and no output after four body timeouts each. Each replay is billed again.

The global undici dispatcher takes `defaultBodyTimeout = 3e5` and `defaultHeadersTimeout = 6e4` from module constants in `packages/core/src/utils/fetch.ts`. The only way to change them is `updateGlobalFetchTimeouts`, driven by the `DEFAULT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` experiment flag, which API-key auth never receives.

#29693 asks for a configurable headers timeout. This issue is the same problem for the body timeout, which a long silent tool call hits even when the first byte arrives in time.

### What did you expect to happen?

A setting or environment variable that raises both the headers and the body timeout under every auth type. Google's Gemini 4 migration checklist (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/latest-model#migration-checklist) recommends client timeouts of at least 15 minutes.

### Client information

- CLI version: 0.64.0
- Auth: Gemini API key
- Model: gemini-4-argon, thinkingLevel HIGH
- OS: Linux (Debian container), Node 22

### Anything else we need to know?

Our workaround rewrites both constants to 1,200,000 ms in the installed bundle (`bundle/chunk-*.js`).

labels.name: priority/p2

labels.name: area/agent

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

In certain cases, the main agent spends many turns, iterations, making incremental changes in hopes of solving a small issue. For example, if a typecheck or linter comes back with numerous failures. The main agent may spend many turns/tokens to help get the build into a healthy state. 

This is one such subtask (also including fixing a broken build) that could be delegated to a subagent such as the generalist to outsource the fix and return to the main agent with a working build. 

Considerations/Objectives:
- Investigate getting the model to use the generalist in subtasks such as this
- evaluate if calling is consistent and provides enough feedback back to the main agent to prevent any hallucinations of state (does the generalist let the main agent know what changes it had to make / if the fix couldn't be fixed without further changes)
- Does the main agent provide enough context for the generalist to successfully accomplish its tasks? Or could this require a way for the main agent to share more context?
- Add behavior evals to see if the behavior is followed consistently.

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

For example, I have "gradle" and "git" skills with descriptions like:
> Executes and manages Gradle builds authoritatively with high-performance background orchestration 
  and surgical failure analysis. This skill is the STRONGLY PREFERRED way 
  to run any Gradle task, providing superior reliability through managed background processes, 
  task-specific output capturing, and deep diagnostic integration. Use it for executing core 
  lifecycle tasks like 'build' or 'assemble', starting persistent development servers, 
  or performing complex build troubleshooting. Do NOT use for specialized test diagnostics 
  (use running_gradle_tests).

and 
> Audits Git repository status, examines history, and implements non-interactive modifications. Processes surgical staging, descriptive commits, and multi-file diff analysis. Use for repository introspection and history-based truth verification. NEVER stages or commits without explicit user directives. Avoids interactive prompts via --no-pager.

that never ever get called when using the relevant tools.

I even have this in my `GEMINI.md` in the "priority rules" section:
> 4. **Agent & Tool Hierarchy:** Whenver considering how to approach a task or do anything, ALWAYS follow the hierarchy of preference: **Sub-Agents** > **Skills** > **Specialized MCP Tools** (NOT a Shell tool or similar) > **General/Builtin Tools** (e.g., `run_shell_command`, `grep_search`, `read_file`).
> 5. **Intentionality Protocol:** Before starting ANY task, you MUST stop and consider which agent, skill, or tool is most appropriate for the specific context. If your plan involves using the shell (even via a tool like `run_shell_command`), you MUST stop and reconsider if a more specialized tool or skill exists to handle the task more reliably.

### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. The agent needs strict grounding in its own documentation to accurately guide users.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

issues.title: /compress command is not persistent across session resume

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/small
labels.description: 1 day or less: trivial logic, UI adjustments, docs

issues.body:
### What happened?

The `/compress` command, which summarizes chat history to save tokens, is not persistent across session exits and resumes. When a user runs `/compress`, the in-memory chat history is correctly replaced by a summary, but this change is not written back to the session file on disk. Consequently, when the session is resumed later (using `--resume` or `/resume`), the CLI loads the original, uncompressed history from the session file, effectively losing the compression.

**Repro Steps:**
1. Start a chat with `gemini`.
2. Build up some history with several messages.
3. Run `/compress` and wait for completion.
4. Exit the CLI.
5. Resume the session with `gemini --resume latest`.
6. Observe that the history has reverted to its uncompressed state.

### What did you expect to happen?

Running `/compress` should persist the compressed history (the summary) to the session file on disk so that subsequent resumes of the same session correctly load the compressed state.

### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

OS: darwin (macOS)
Version: Current (detected in local development)

</details>

### Login information

N/A (General bug in persistence logic)

### Anything else we need to know?

Investigation shows that in `packages/core/src/core/client.ts`, the `tryCompressChat` method correctly replaces the `this.chat` object with a new `GeminiChat` initialized with the compressed history:
```typescript
this.chat = await this.startChat(newHistory, resumedData);
```
However, the `ChatRecordingService` (which manages the session file) is initialized with `resumedData` (which points to the existing session file) but is not explicitly instructed to overwrite the file's message history with the new `newHistory`. The `initialize` method in `ChatRecordingService` merely points to the existing file without clearing or updating its messages.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

Linked Draft PR: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/pull/18924

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

issues.body:
Currently all subagents today get a `complete_task` tool. For subagents that do not have or want a more complex return schema, an absence of schema could be used to omit this tool. In this case, the subagent is considered finished when no more tool calls are made. 

Considerations:
- The model could return with less helpful or no response text at all. In this case, there is a less useful handoff. 
- Ensure this does not reduce quality for any built-in subagents
- Behavior may vary by model

Ideally, we can support both completions via the tool and without depending on the schema used.

prs.title: fix(core): fix detectPowerShellSubstitution quote tracking and false positives
prs.body:
## Summary
Fixes false positive command substitution detection in `detectPowerShellSubstitution` on Windows.
When quotes or escaped characters were present within double-quoted strings (such as `\"`, `""`, or nested single quotes), the parser's `inDoubleQuote` state tracking desynchronized, causing legitimate commands with parentheses (like `git log --format="%h \" (%an)"` or `git commit -m "fix(core): \"quoted\" (detail)"`) to be falsely blocked with a command injection warning.

## Details
1. **Quote State Machine Tracking**:
   - Inside single quotes: In PowerShell, `''` escapes a single quote; handle doubled single quotes `''` without exiting single quote mode.
   - Inside double quotes: In PowerShell, `""` escapes a double quote; handle doubled double quotes `""` without exiting double quote mode.
   - Backslash escape handling: Windows executables and wrappers frequently escape quotes as `\"`. In double quotes, consume backslash escape sequences `['$', '`', '"', '\\', '(', ')', "'"]` via `i += 2` so `\"` does not prematurely toggle `inDoubleQuote` to `false`.
   - Outside quotes: Handle general escape sequences (`\` and `` ` ``) so escaped parens like `\(` are not flagged as unquoted subexpressions.
2. **Regression Testing**:
   - Added unit test suite in `packages/core/src/utils/shell-utils.test.ts` testing escaped double quotes with parens, doubled quotes, escaped substitution syntax, and verifying that actual malicious subexpressions (`$()`, `@()`, bare `()`) remain strictly blocked.
   - Added regression test in `packages/core/src/tools/shell.test.ts` verifying end-to-end execution of PowerShell commands with nested/escaped quotes and parentheses.

## Related Issues
Fixes #29738

## How to Validate
1. Run PowerShell with nested quotes and parentheses:
   ```powershell
   git commit -m "fix(core): \"quoted\" (detail)"
   git log --format="%h \" (%an)"
   echo "a \" b (c)"
   ```
   **Expected**: Commands execute cleanly without being blocked by command injection detection.
2. Run command injection attempts:
   ```powershell
   echo (whoami)
   echo $(whoami)
   echo @(whoami)
   ```
   **Expected**: Blocked with command injection warning.
3. Run test suites:
   - `packages/core/src/utils/shell-utils.test.ts`
   - `packages/core/src/tools/shell.test.ts`

prs.title: fix(cli): handle response and write stream errors in extension downloadFile
prs.body:
## Summary

`downloadFile()` in `packages/cli/src/config/extensions/github.ts` now handles failures from the HTTP response stream and from the destination write stream, instead of relying on `finish` alone: the returned promise rejects exactly once, both streams are torn down, and the partially written archive is removed.

Fixes #28645.

## Details

Before this change `downloadFile()` piped the response into `fs.createWriteStream(dest)` and listened only for `finish`, with no `error` listener on either stream. Because of that:

- A response that failed **after** the headers arrived (mid-transfer network failure), or a write failure such as `ENOSPC`/`EACCES`, emitted an `error` event with no listener — an unhandled `EventEmitter` error — instead of rejecting the returned promise, so `downloadFromGitHubRelease()` never reported a failed download and installation could hang.
- The partially written archive stayed at `dest` for a later extraction/install to pick up.

The fix keeps the existing manual `Promise` wrapper (rather than `stream/promises.pipeline()`, the other option suggested in the issue) because it is the smallest diff that produces the same end state:

- `settled`/"once" guards so the first failure (or success) wins and later events on either stream are ignored.
- On failure: `res.unpipe(file)` and `file.destroy()` stop the download and release the file handle.
- The incomplete archive is unlinked from the write stream's `close` handler, so removal happens after the handle is released (avoids `EBUSY`/`EPERM` on Windows).
- `removeIncompleteDownload()` is best-effort: the file may never have been created.

## Related Issues

Fixes #28645

## How to Validate

```
cd packages/cli
npx vitest run src/config/extensions/github.test.ts
```

Result: `Test Files 1 passed (1)`, `Tests 37 passed (37)`.

New regression tests in `packages/cli/src/config/extensions/github.test.ts` under `describe('downloadFile')`:

- response stream error after a `200` → rejects with that error, calls `unpipe`/`destroy`, and unlinks the destination once the stream has closed;
- write stream error (`ENOSPC`) → rejects with that error, destroys the stream, and unlinks the destination;
- a failure that arrives after the first one → the promise still rejects with the first error, and no error is thrown as unhandled.

Also run:

- `npx eslint packages/cli/src/config/extensions/github.ts packages/cli/src/config/extensions/github.test.ts --max-warnings 0` → exit 0, no warnings.
- `npm run typecheck -w @google/gemini-cli` → `tsc --noEmit`, exit 0.

Not run: full `npm run preflight` (clean + install + build + all workspace tests) — the targeted checks above cover the touched package. End-to-end validation of a real interrupted download was not performed; the suite asserts the failure paths against mocked streams.

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [ ] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed) — not needed; no user-facing change beyond correct error propagation and no longer leaving a partial archive.
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Noted breaking changes (if any) — none: the success path is unchanged, and callers already treat a rejection as `failureReason: 'failed to download asset'`.
- [x] Validated on required platforms/methods:
  - [ ] MacOS
    - [ ] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
    - [ ] Podman
    - [ ] Seatbelt
  - [x] Windows
    - [x] npm run (unit tests, typecheck and lint above)
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
