issues.title: [Bug]: Slack native task cards: a tool that finishes after 8 newer tool calls started stays "in progress"
issues.body:
### Description

The native task-card lane (since #85476) publishes `_TaskCardState.visible_tasks()`, the 8 most recently started tasks (`task_order[-8:]` in `gateway/run_turn_runner.py`). A status change to an older task is applied to the state but never sent to `send_native_task_card_progress`. When a turn issues 9 or more parallel tool calls, the first ones finish outside that window, and the card keeps the "in progress" status it last received for them.

### Steps to Reproduce

On `main` (`d97007c32d`):

```python
from gateway.run_turn_runner import TurnRunner

card = TurnRunner._TaskCardState(adapter=None)
for n in range(9):
    card.apply_event({"type": "tool.started", "tool_call_id": f"call-{n}", "tool_name": "web_search"})
card.apply_event({"type": "tool.completed", "tool_call_id": "call-0", "tool_name": "web_search"})
print([task["id"] for task in card.visible_tasks()])
# ['call-1', ..., 'call-8']: the frame published for call-0's completion does not contain call-0
```

### Expected Behavior

Every status change reaches the adapter, so each task ends in its final state on the card.

### Actual Behavior

`call-0`'s completion is never published.

### Proposed Fix

Remember which tasks changed since the last successful native publish and send the ones outside the window along with it. PR to follow.

issues.title: feat(memory): budget enforcement and an acceptance pipeline at write time for MEMORY.md / USER.md

labels.name: type/feature
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: tool/memory
labels.description: Memory tool and memory providers

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Low — cosmetic, nice to have

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

labels.name: area/memory
labels.description: Memory subsystem: store, providers, sync, background reviews

issues.body:
Need (general)
`MEMORY.md` / `USER.md` are injected into EVERY future turn — they are latency and cost on every
session. Today nothing in the product governs what goes IN: no size budget, no acceptance test at
write time, no distinction between "facts that apply to every session" (belong in memory) and
"procedures/lessons for a recurring task type" (belong in skills), and no automatic consequence when
the store approaches its cap. Result in the field: memory accretes into a second, worse session
history — stale facts, imperative phrasing that hijacks later sessions, duplicated procedures — and
the curation pass becomes a manual archaeology exercise.

## Proposed core behaviour
1. **Budget enforcement at write time.** A configurable character cap per store (memory/user).
   Writes that would cross a soft threshold (e.g. 85%) must displace existing content or route to an
   overflow document — never silently grow the injected context.
2. **Acceptance pipeline on every memory edit** (adds AND rewrites): shape check (declarative facts,
   not instructions — imperative phrasing rejected with a hint), semantic check (fits the store's
   purpose: facts that apply to every session; task procedures belong in skills), and staleness
   awareness (facts dated within a short window flagged as session-log material).
3. **Change log.** Every admit / remove / consolidate / refusal appends one line (action + rationale)
   to a machine-readable log the user can audit.
4. **Consequence hooks.** Refusals return a structured error naming the rule violated and where the
   content should live instead (e.g. "write this as a skill"), so the agent can reroute rather than
   retry blindly.

## Why core, not plugin
Plugins can veto memory tool calls via `pre_tool_call`, and that is how the reference implementation
works — but the budget is core state (the store is core-owned), the clean integration point is the
memory writer itself, and every heavy user of memory otherwise rebuilds this pipeline independently.
A core implementation also lets the budget feed the same telemetry surface as context size (#26382
family).

**Tests (generic):**
- Over-cap write is refused (or routed to overflow) with a structured error; the store's measured
  size never exceeds the cap after any sequence of writes.
- An imperative-phrased entry is rejected with the shape hint; the corrected declarative form
  passes.
- A procedure-shaped entry (recurring-task instructions) is rejected with a "belongs in skills" hint.
- Every accepted/rejected write appends exactly one change-log line.

**Prior art check (8 Oct 2026):** #69264 (memory-hygiene SKILL for curation) and #116673
(MEMORY.md anchor chains) address the CONTENT lifecycle; #25309 (dreaming/consolidation) addresses
background rewriting. None enforces budget + acceptance at the moment of writing — the gap above.

issues.title: Cannot open a pull request via API: CreatePullRequest permission error (issue creation and fork PRs still work)

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area/auth
labels.description: Authentication, OAuth, credential pools

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

labels.name: blocked
labels.description: Waiting on external dependency or decision

issues.body:
## What happens

Opening a pull request against this repository from our fork fails, for our account only. Exact errors, reproduced twice within two minutes (2026-10-03 00:14–00:16 UTC):

```
gh pr create --repo NousResearch/hermes-agent --head kuehnberger:fix/aux-cost-provenance-v2 --base main
→ GraphQL: kuehnberger does not have the correct permissions to execute `CreatePullRequest`

gh api -X POST repos/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls -f title=… -f head=kuehnberger:fix/aux-cost-provenance-v2 -f base=main
→ HTTP 404 {"message":"Not Found"}
```

## What still works for the same token / same account

| action | endpoint | result |
|---|---|---|
| create an issue here | `POST /repos/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues` | 201, works (used as a probe, then closed) |
| create a PR on our own fork | `POST /repos/kuehnberger/hermes-agent/pulls` | 201, works (PR #2 in the fork) |
| push branches to our fork | `git push fork` | works |
| read this repo, compare heads, read our 4 open PRs | REST/GraphQL | works |
| cross-repo compare of the new branch | `GET /compare/main...kuehnberger:fix/aux-cost-provenance-v2` | works (`diverged`) |

Repository permissions returned for our account on this repo: `admin=false push=false triage=false`. Token scopes: `repo`, `workflow`, `notifications`, `read:org`, `gist`.

## Controls (to rule out the obvious causes)

- **Not a GitHub incident** — githubstatus.com reports all systems operational, Pull Requests `Normal`.
- **Not repo-wide**: other accounts, including first-timers with `author_association: NONE`, opened PRs here at 00:06, 00:07, 00:12 and 00:13 UTC — i.e. within the same minutes that our attempt failed (00:14–00:16 UTC).
- **Not a block**: `GET /repos/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blocks/kuehnberger` → 404 (not blocked), same for the org endpoint.
- **Not a broken fork link**: our fork reports `fork: true`, `parent: NousResearch/hermes-agent`, `archived: false`, `disabled: false`.
- **Not an existing PR** for this head: `GET /pulls?head=kuehnberger:fix/aux-cost-provenance-v2` → empty.
- **Not interaction limits**: issue creation succeeded with the same credentials, minutes ago.

Our last successful PR creation here was https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/127847 on 2026-09-29.

## Impact

One branch is ready and waiting: `kuehnberger:fix/aux-cost-provenance-v2` (4 files, +89/−0, 2 commits, `fix(usage): persist cost provenance on auxiliary-usage rows`, tests green on `main` `4e3fcd5cd7`). Its description is written; only the "Create pull request" step fails.

Our four existing open PRs are unaffected — we only comment/rebase them, and those API calls still work.

## Ask

Is PR creation currently restricted for external accounts (or for this account/fork in particular)? If the restriction is intentional, a sentence saying so is plenty and we'll stop retrying. If it isn't intentional, any pointer to what changed would help — the error message reads like a permissions check rather than a rate limit, which is why we can't diagnose it from outside.

Happy to move the branch out of the way, or to open the PR through another path, if that's easier.



---

## Consolidated roll-call table (maintained)

Moved into this description on 2026-10-11 because long issue timelines collapse older comments behind "Load more" — the table was unreachable without clicking through 69 hidden items. This section is now the single source of truth; the old table comment is edited to a pointer. Facts last re-verified 2026-10-10 18:14 UTC (unchanged since; see https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/131859#issuecomment-6104028526 for the 10-11 additions). Row 15 (@devtroniu) added 2026-10-11 from https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/135444 (embedded self-report, never posted here); account column now @-mentions each account so everyone listed gets one notification. Row 14 (1052326311) added 2026-10-11 03:50 UTC from https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/131859#issuecomment-6104594125 — every fact in it verified against the pulls API the same hour (PR #136041 author/draft-state/creation-time match the report). **Row 17 (@PRELVAS94) added 2026-10-13 from https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/131859#issuecomment-6129616866.** Facts re-verified 2026-10-14 05:3x CEST.

**The gate is scoped to this repository, not to our accounts (10-12…10-13, three independent accounts).** The decisive test is a zero-side-effect cross-repo probe: `POST /repos/<repo>/pulls` with a head ref that does not exist. A `404` means the creation gate refused the request; a `422 Validation Failed` means the permission check passed and only the invalid head failed. @Finn763 ran it first (10-12): `NousResearch/hermes-agent` → **404**, four unrelated public repos → **422**. @686f6c61 replicated it the same day on a second account: `NousResearch/hermes-agent` → **404**, two private org repos where he has push → **422**. @PRELVAS94 replicated it on a **third** account (10-13 23:4x UTC): non-draft `NousResearch/hermes-agent` → **404**, the same repo with `draft: true` → **422**, their own fork → **422**, `octocat/Hello-World` → **422** — one variable (the draft flag) apart on the same repository and token. So the gate follows the repository, not the account, on three independent accounts. This also re-frames the onset clustering: the 10-02/03 onset across accounts is real, but it cannot be a platform-wide account throttle — it looks like a repo-scoped enforcement that switched on around 10-02/03. Anyone can run the probe; it is the one test that ends the "is it us?" debate.

**The cap is a documented GitHub feature — and its behavior matches our observations exactly.** GitHub shipped "Limit open pull requests for users without write access" on 2026-06-17: *"If a user without write access reaches the limit, they'll need to close or merge an existing pull request before opening another one. You can also add trusted contributors to a bypass list, allowing them to exceed the limit without being granted full collaborator access. **Draft pull requests do not count towards a user's limit.**"* ([changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-06-17-limit-open-pull-requests-for-users-without-write-access/)) That last sentence is the draft exemption every account in this table reports, and the greyed-button tooltip — *"Author has reached the open pull request limit"* — is this feature's message. The remedy is a **bypass list**, maintainer-only: GraphQL `addPullRequestCreationCapBypassUsers` — *"Bypassed users can create pull requests regardless of the configured cap. Only users with maintainer permissions can manage the bypass list. You can add a maximum of 100 users per request."* ([docs](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/pulls)). The config itself is admin-only (`pullRequestCreationCapConfig` — *"Only visible to repository maintainers and administrators"*), which is why our `GET /interaction-limits/pulls/creation-cap` returns 403.

**The gate is not static — it lifts intermittently (10-13).** @PRELVAS94 created **five non-draft pull requests here in a six-minute window on 2026-10-13, 16:51:39–16:57:56Z** (#137917, #137918, #137920, #137922 non-draft, plus #137921 as a draft), each closed again within ~20 seconds as deliberate throwaway tests. By 23:4x UTC the same probe was back to a stable 404 across three consecutive rounds. The confound, stated rather than hidden: their own session was running a cap experiment during that exact window (one of their PRs was closed for ~30 s and reopened), so the burst is consistent with **either** a count-based cap that happened to have a free slot **or** an intermittent lift — it is posted as a timeline observation, not as proof of either. What is solid either way: creation succeeded in a six-minute window on 10-13 and failed again ~7 hours later on the same account with the same token. This matches @Ieqzya's 10-08 two-PR window in shape, and it is the first evidence that the enforcement state changes on its own, on this repository, without anything an account does.

**What is still unexplained: the threshold, the bypass list, and the intermittency.** A count cap cannot explain an account creating non-draft PRs freely at ~54 non-draft open while another is gated at 3 — unless the high-volume collaborators are on the bypass list. The coherent story is a cap enabled or lowered on this repository around 2026-10-02/03, with the frequent collaborators bypassed. No GitHub status incident matches that window (the Oct 7 and Oct 12 incidents are resolved and unrelated; the Oct 02 changelog entry is "Stateless GitHub App installation tokens"), so this reads as a configuration change rather than an outage.

**Refined maintainer ask (one line):** is `pullRequestCreationCapConfig` enabled on this repository, at what threshold, and can the 17 affected accounts be added to the bypass list?

**Parallel track — GitHub Support tickets.** Each affected account should file its **own** ticket, in its own words, from its own facts (no shared template, no cross-referencing — a coordinated campaign reads as abuse, while N independent tickets from N accounts with the same onset and the same 404 read as a pattern Support can route). The substantive ask is the same four questions for all. Roll-call #2 was answered by 1 of the 8 pinged (yuzilongleif-collab); Finn763 and ranggaoscar reported unprompted. Roll-call #3 below re-pings the silent names. Nobody has reported a resolution at any point. Roll-call #3 (posted 2026-10-10 18:15 UTC) has been answered so far by 1052326311 (row 14).

**The tooltip — the one hard datum nobody had.** Finn763 reports the greyed *Ready for review* button's tooltip verbatim: **"Author has reached the open pull request limit"**, and names the repository config `repository.pullRequestCreationCapConfig` (with `pullRequestCreationPolicy` = `ALL`), noting drafts do not count toward the cap — which is exactly the split every account reports. This is the first direct, account-side observation of the cap message; AgilityHacker proposed the cap as a hypothesis on 10-03 and maebahesioru corroborated. We cannot read the config ourselves: `GET /repos/NousResearch/hermes-agent/interaction-limits/pulls/creation-cap` returns **403 "Must have admin rights"** for a non-maintainer token (re-checked 10-10), which is itself part of why this needs a maintainer.

**Counter-example, re-measured 10-10 (replaces the stale one).** The cap theory predicts that an account far above the limit cannot create non-draft PRs. Two independent accounts have now also tested the reverse: @PRATHAMESH75 (68 open, closed down from 81) and @686f6c61 (58 open, closed down from 81) each closed dozens of PRs — the gate did not move, so the open-PR count is not the lever. `kshitijk4poor` holds **67 open PRs** and created **non-draft** PRs at 10-10 09:16–09:19 UTC (#136053, #136051, #136050 — all `draft=false`), i.e. within hours of this census. Either he is on the bypass list or open-PR count alone is not the gate. (An earlier revision of this table cited "61 open non-draft"; the measured number today is 67 open, of which a 10-PR sample was 8 non-draft / 2 draft.) **A second, independent falsification (10-12):** the last successful non-draft create clusters on 10-02 for at least six accounts, with onset 10-03 for all of them — while those accounts sit at 4, 58, 68 and 563→50 open PRs. A count cap cannot fire simultaneously across counts differing by two orders of magnitude, and it cannot survive three close-down experiments (81→58, 81→68, 563→50) that changed nothing. @Finn763's recommendation: stop the close-downs — the data says they are not the lever — and aim GitHub Support at this repository's cap config. **A third falsification (10-13):** @686f6c61 holds **75 open PRs here — 48 non-draft, 27 draft** — and non-draft creation has been refused continuously since #131384 on 10-02. 48 non-draft open is therefore not above whatever the threshold is, or the threshold is not a plain count of open non-draft PRs.

**Maintainer shortcuts (each verifiable in under a minute):**
1. **The cap config** — `repository.pullRequestCreationCapConfig` / `pullRequestCreationPolicy` on this repo, plus `GET /interaction-limits/pulls/bypass-list`. The one-line answer "the cap is N, here is the bypass list" would settle it. (Finn763's tooltip, above.)
2. **Ruled out: it is not simply open-PR count** — see the kshitijk4poor counter-example above.
3. **Repro on any affected account** — non-draft `POST /repos/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls` → 404, `draft: true` → 201; `markPullRequestReadyForReview` → FORBIDDEN (verbatim rejections linked per row).
4. **Our two drafts with the greyed button**: [#106973](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/106973), [#103311](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/103311).
5. **A maintainer-side flip is refused too** — teknium1: *"GitHub also refused a maintainer `ready` on this draft, so we landed your approved pin (`f65e62d1`, 0.1.8) through salvage PR [#135484](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/135484) ... Closing this one in favour of it."* https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/131859#issuecomment-6076812882 — i.e. the ready-flip is refused on the author side **and** the maintainer side, and an approved, uncontroversial catalog pin had to be re-landed through a salvage PR.
6. **The one test that ends the "is it us?" debate** — the cross-repo probe above (zero side effect): `POST /repos/<repo>/pulls` with a head ref that does not exist. `404` = the creation gate refused; `422 Validation Failed` = the permission check passed and only the invalid head failed. Run it on any repo you have push rights to. Replicated on two independent accounts 10-12 (see the paragraph above the table).

**Pre-wall non-draft PRs still open (timeline markers).** [#123155](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/123155) (atzx, non-draft, open since 09-25 — the carrier 686f6c61 stood down for in favour of it) and [#130744](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/130744) / [#129284](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/129284) (deadczarvc, non-draft, open since 09-30/10-01). Non-draft PRs created before the wall stay open and unaffected; the gate applies to *creating* them and to the ready-flip.

**Census (re-measured 2026-10-10 17:5x UTC):** **22 open PRs by 10 distinct authors** cite this issue as the reason for their draft status — measured draft split **21 draft / 1 non-draft** (the non-draft is [#135190](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/135190), Akloenx123). Authors: 33hodl (7), ruizanthony (3), Akloenx123 (3), thatssoheil (2), ranggaoscar (2), maebahesioru, dwaxe, benjaminbrumbaugh, yuzilongleif-collab, 1052326311. Newly citing since the previous census: 1052326311 ([#136041](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/136041)), yuzilongleif-collab ([#135370](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/135370)), ranggaoscar ([#136062](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/136062), [#136095](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/136095)), dwaxe ([#135833](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/135833)), Akloenx123 ([#136103](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/136103)). Two authors named in the previous census (ericcurtin, yoyodine-industries) no longer have any citing open PR — either their PRs closed or the citation was dropped; they are not pinged below.

Still no other issue tracks this (title scan for `CreatePullRequest`: exactly one hit — this one), so this stays the tracker.

**Caveat on this census:** GitHub search returned 22 items but the per-item listing yielded 21 in one pull; treat 22 as the authoritative total and the per-author counts as a floor. Search also never returns `pull_request.draft`, which is why the draft split above was measured per PR through the pulls API rather than read off the search result.

issues.title: whatsapp_cloud: allowlist strips every non-digit, so business-scoped user ids (BSUIDs) can collide
issues.body:
**Where:** `gateway/platforms/whatsapp_cloud.py` (checked on `main` at d97007c32d and tag v2026.9.24): `_normalize_allow_ids` and `_entry_matches`.

```python
return {re.sub(r"\D", "", entry.split("@", 1)[0]) or entry for entry in ids}
...
bare = re.sub(r"\D", "", str(target).split("@", 1)[0]) or target
return bare in self._normalize_allow_ids(entries) or super()._entry_matches(entries, target)
```

**Problem:** since the 2026 WhatsApp usernames rollout, the Cloud API's `messages[].from` (and `contacts[].wa_id`) can carry a business-scoped user id (BSUID, `CC.<alphanumeric>`, e.g. `DE.1A2B3C4D5E`) instead of a phone number. `sender_id = raw_message["from"]` (around L835 / L1014) then goes through the digit-only normalisation, and so do allowlist entries. Two different BSUIDs whose digits are the same in the same order become the same bare id:

```
DE.1A2B3C4D5E -> 12345
DE.12345ABCDE -> 12345
```

So an allowlist that names one user's BSUID admits any sender whose BSUID shares its digit projection. The same applies to the interactive-tap check (`_dispatch_interactive_reply` -> `_is_dm_allowed`), which gates approval buttons. The odds for a long random BSUID are small, but the comparison is wrong by construction, and short digit projections (a BSUID that is mostly letters) collide easily. Entries also lose their country prefix, and a BSUID with no digits at all falls back to its raw form, so the matcher treats two id types inconsistently.

**Suggested fix:** normalise only values that are phone ids (strip `+`, spaces and `@...` JID suffixes, then require `^[1-9][0-9]{5,14}$`); compare anything shaped like a BSUID (`^[A-Z]{2}\.[A-Za-z0-9]{1,128}$`) byte for byte, case-sensitive; never cross-match a BSUID against a phone entry. Also consider reading the BSUID from `contacts[].user_id` / `from_user_id` when `from` is a phone number, so an operator can allowlist by BSUID once users hide their numbers. A regression test with the two ids above would pin it.

Context: found while designing an owner-only WhatsApp line for a self-hosted Hermes; we compare exactly on our side in the meantime. Happy to open a PR if useful.

issues.title: ACP: no plan update for todo_list (todo → todo_list rename), and none at all through the tool_call bridge

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/acp
labels.description: Agent Communication Protocol adapter

labels.name: P4
labels.description: Best-effort: we will get to it when we get to it (no commitment)

issues.body:
## Summary

Since the `todo` → `todo_list` and `process` → `process_manage` renames, the ACP adapter still keys on the old names:

1. **No plan update is ever sent.** ACP clients' native task panel (`sessionUpdate: "plan"`) stops updating.
2. **Both tools lose their curated rendering.** Kind, start content and result formatting fall back to the generic path. `process_manage` is reported as kind `other` instead of `execute`.

## Where it happens

`acp_adapter/events.py` (`make_step_cb`) and `acp_adapter/server.py` (`_history_replay_updates`) emit the plan only for the old name:

```python
if tool_name == "todo" and (plan_update := _build_plan_update_from_todo_result(result)) is not None:
```

`acp_adapter/tools.py` registers `todo` / `process` only, in `TOOL_KIND_MAP`, `_POLISHED_TOOLS`, `_COMPLETION_FORMATTERS` and `_START_CONTENT_BUILDERS`.

## Accepting the new name in the step callback is not enough

When `todo_list` is deferred behind `tool_search`, the model calls it through the `tool_call` bridge. The step callback reads names from the assistant's wire `tool_calls` (`_previous_tool_round`), so it sees `tool_call`, never `todo_list`. History replay has the same problem: the stored assistant `tool_calls` carry `tool_call`, while the tool row's `tool_name` is `todo_list`.

`tool.completed` is the one place that sees the unwrapped name: `agent/tool_executor.py` emits it after `_unwrap_tool_search_call`.

## Reproduction

1. Run `hermes acp` with tool discovery on, so non-core tools sit behind `tool_search`.
2. Ask for a multi-step task tracked with the todo tool (e.g. "make a 10-step todo list, then complete each step, marking it completed").
3. Observe the session updates: `todo_list` tool calls arrive, but no `sessionUpdate: "plan"` does. On 0.21.0, with the old `todo` name, the plan was emitted.

## Expected

One plan update per completed `todo_list` call, carrying the full list. Curated start/result rendering for `todo_list` and `process_manage`, same as before the rename.

## Environment

Hermes v0.21.7 (`71d34bad`) and current `main` (`d97007c32d`), via `hermes acp`, Linux.

## Proposed fix

PR to follow:
- Send the plan from `close_tool_call`, on `tool.completed`, using `tools.todo_tool.is_todo_tool_name`.
- Keep the step-callback emission only on its fallback path, where it closed the call itself.
- In history replay, also check the stored `tool_name`.
- Register the new names in the four tables, keeping the old names for replayed transcripts.

prs.title: fix(deps): httpx2 / httpcore2 2.12.0 clears five advisories on the MCP HTTP stack (salvage #116210)
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

mcp 2.0 builds its HTTP transports on httpx2, so every HTTP MCP connection ran on 2.7.0, which has five published advisories. 2.12.0 is the first release that clears all of them; OSV lists no advisories for httpx2 or httpcore2 at 2.12.0.

Part of a stack on [#138006](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/138006): #138006 → #138024 → #138025 → #138026 → #138027 → #138028. Each PR touches different files; the order is not a dependency.

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)

```sh
python -m pm.build_env --source . --check-lock
```

## Verification

## What does this PR do?

`hermes doctor` reported 3 / 8 / 6 npm findings for the root, web and ui-tui trees and 2 more for the WhatsApp bridge. After this change all four audit at 0. The pinned overrides stop `npm audit fix` from persisting, so the committed lockfile is the only durable fix; Docker users get it by pulling an image rebuilt from it.

Part of a stack on [#138006](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/138006): #138006 → #138024 → #138025 → #138026 → #138027 → #138028. Each PR touches different files; the order is not a dependency.

## Related Issue

## Type of Change

1. #136789's pins: `brace-expansion` 5.0.12, `js-yaml` 4.3.2, `undici` 6.29.0 / 7.30.0, `yaml` 2.9.1, `vitest` + `@vitest/mocker` 4.1.11, with the lock to match.
2. `source-map-js` 1.2.2 (the last web/ui-tui finding). 1.2.2 was published 2026-09-30, inside `min-release-age=14`, so `.npmrc` excludes it by name like the other advisory fixes, with a note to remove the line once it is older than two weeks. 4. `scripts/whatsapp-bridge/package-lock.json`: lock-only bump of `sharp` 0.35.5 (high, bundled librsvg CVE-2026-96889) and `music-metadata` 11.16.1 (moderate). Every moved version was published 2026-09-27 or earlier.

## Credit

@sajidhaleem wrote the dependency bump (#136789); their commit is cherry-picked unchanged. The `source-map-js`, pin-sync and bridge commits are mine.

## Overlapping open PRs

prs.title: feat(release): dispatch Stable Release from the default branch
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Stable Release now runs from the default branch, like Canary already does. The claim tag is an input. Before, every stable run was dispatched on its own claim tag.

**The problem.** GitHub Actions caches belong to the ref a run is dispatched on. A cache saved on `rc.14-v0.21.7` cannot be read by `rc.15-v0.21.7`. So no stable run ever reused a cache. In the last green run (rc.15, run 38199200509, 112 minutes) all three native legs logged `Cache not found` for the dependency cache, the electron-builder cache and the signature cache. rc.14 had saved the exact same key prefix two hours earlier. The cost of that:

| Leg | Cold work in that run |
|---|---|
| win32-x64 | 812 payload files signed with 0 cache hits (~13 min), 240 Python packages prepared in 5m30 |
| win32-arm64 | 768 payload files signed with 0 cache hits (~17 min), vcpkg OpenSSL build (~3 min), source builds of cryptography and others |
| darwin-arm64 | Nothing to gain. Apple notarization alone took 23 min |

This PR does not make macOS faster. It lets the Windows legs reuse work between attempts.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Dispatch ref | `refs/tags/<claim>` | `refs/heads/main`, claim tag in the `tag` input |
| Cache scope | one private scope per claim | main's scope, shared by all claims |
| `GITHUB_SHA` | the claim commit | main's tip |
| Commit under test | `GITHUB_SHA` | resolved from the claim tag at admission, passed to every lane |
| Workflows and release scripts | from the claim commit | from main |

## Changes Made

Commit 1, `ci(release): pass the commit under test through every stable lane`

- 34 reusable workflows reachable from `stable-release.yml` gain an optional `commit` input. Their checkouts use it. An empty input keeps PR and push behavior the same. `pm-bundle.yml` and `desktop-bundle-smoke.yml` keep the `ref` and `sha` inputs they already had.
- `tests/ci/test_stable_release_commit_threading.py` walks that workflow graph. It fails when a lane cannot take a commit, a call does not forward it, or a checkout ignores it. Without it, a missed checkout would test main's tip and still go green.
- The `*-packaged` jobs now need `admit` directly. A job only sees the outputs of its direct `needs`, so they would have read an empty commit.

Commit 2, `feat(release): dispatch Stable Release from the default branch`

- `stable.check_claim` takes the commit from the claim tag. It requires a `workflow_dispatch` of `stable-release.yml` on `refs/heads/main` instead of `GITHUB_REF` and `GITHUB_SHA`. The tag must still be annotated, match the remote object, match the claim epoch, and be an ancestor of `origin/main`.
- The protected publisher accepts `stable-release.yml@refs/heads/<default>` instead of the claim tag ref.
- `release.py` and the release entrypoint dispatch on the default branch.
- `abandon` and the sequencer found a claim's runs by `headBranch == claim tag`. Every run now has `headBranch=main`, so they match the run name `Stable release <tag>`. Runs that started on the tag still match (`stable.is_claim_run`).
- `stable-publish` and `stable-store` set `RELEASE_COMMIT` to the admitted commit. `release_artifacts` reads it before `GITHUB_SHA`.
- The stable-releases doc describes the new flow.

Commit 3, `fix(release): keep a stable run on main from using the controller commit or cancelling pushes` (review round 1)

- A stable run is on main, so a push to main could cancel its checks. 14 nested workflows keyed their concurrency group on the ref or on "tag". They now use the run id when the caller passes a commit, and do not cancel those runs.
- `docker.yml` and `nix.yml` archived, stamped and labelled `GITHUB_SHA`. They now use `CANDIDATE_COMMIT` (the commit input, or the triggering commit).
- The install e2e manifest check compared against `GITHUB_SHA`. It now reads `HERMES_TESTED_COMMIT`.
- `e2e-desktop.yml` rewrote the visual baselines whenever the ref was main. A stable run now only compares and never writes them.
- The lint test also checks the value each nested call passes, every concurrency group, and any other use of the triggering ref or SHA. Each allowed use has a reason in the test.

## What this does not do

- It does not guard against drift between main's workflows and the claim commit. Main's scripts are wanted here.
- Jobs that run controller scripts (`transitions`, `acceptance`, `publication`, `complete`, the phase gates) stay on main on purpose.
- `desktop-bundle-smoke.yml` is unchanged. It already tests the staged artifact of `sha` with the dispatched ref's scripts.
- A claim cut from a commit before this PR fails admission, because that commit's scripts still require the tag ref. Only new claims work.
- Cache writes from stable runs now land in main's scope. The environments `release-signing`, `container-publish` and `trusted-automation` already allow `main`, which I checked with the API.

## How to Test

Not yet proven in CI. A real dispatch is the test:

1. After merge, cut a claim and dispatch it: `gh workflow run stable-release.yml --ref main -f tag=<claim tag>`. Admission refuses any other ref, so the branch cannot be dispatched before merge.
2. In the first run, check the cache save lines for `desktop-inputs-v1-*` and `payload-signatures-v1-*`. Their ref must be `refs/heads/...`.
3. Dispatch a second claim and check that the same keys log `Cache restored` and that `[batch-sign]` reports cache hits.

Local checks:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Commit-threading lint (6 tests) and the stable graph test (14) | pass |
| `tests/scripts/test_stable_release.py` | 40 pass |
| Release, entrypoint, sequencer, channel, admission tests (27 files) | 418 pass, 2 fail |
| `actionlint` on the changed workflows, compared with `origin/main` | no new findings |

The 2 failing files (`test_release_revision_anchor.py`, `test_release_tag_sampling.py`) fail the same way on a clean `origin/main`. So do 82 tests in `test_update_ci_routing.py`, `test_update_transitive_routing.py` and `test_prompt_surface.py` (`tee: command not found` in the scrubbed environment).

prs.title: Docker plugin installs no longer rebuild python-olm from source
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

A new PM environment generation in the Docker image, for example a plugin install, no longer rebuilds python-olm from source: the image now ships its uv cache at the path PM seeds from.

The image build runs `pm.build_env` as root before `ENV HERMES_HOME` is set, so uv's cache went to `/root/.hermes/cache/uv`. At runtime `pm.packages.uv_cache_dir()` returns `$HERMES_HOME/cache/uv` (`/opt/data/cache/uv`, an empty volume path) and seeds it only from `/opt/hermes/uv-cache`, which the image never created. python-olm has no cp313 or cp314 wheel, so every generation that includes it compiled it.

## Related Issue

No issue exists. A user report of python-olm compiling "on first boot" led here. First boot of the published image does not compile it (checked on `rc.15-v0.21.7`); a new generation does.

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)

## Changes Made

- `Dockerfile`: pass `--cache /opt/hermes/uv-cache` to the `pm.build_env` call in `python_deps`, with a comment that says why the default is wrong.
- `pm/packages.py`: `uv_cache_dir()` records `+payload` in `.seeded` when a payload cache is present. An image without a seed still wrote the marker for its lock, so an existing volume skipped the merge when a later image with the same lock added the seed (review finding).
- `tests/pm/test_uv_cache_seed.py`: one test for that case. It fails without the `pm/packages.py` change.

## How to Test

Same `pm.build_env` command, `--extra matrix`, fresh output dir, runtime cache dir from `uv_cache_dir()`, `--cpus=2`:

| Image | Result |
|---|---|
| `nousresearch/hermes-agent:rc.15-v0.21.7` (no seed) | 50.0 s |
| this branch, `docker build --target runtime` | 2.7 s |

1. `docker build --target runtime -t hermes-agent:uv-seed .`
2. `docker run --rm --cpus=2 --entrypoint /bin/bash hermes-agent:uv-seed -c 'cd /opt/hermes; C=$(.venv/bin/python -c "from pm.packages import uv_cache_dir;print(uv_cache_dir())"); python3 -m pm.build_env --source /opt/hermes --python /usr/local/bin/python3 --cache $C --out /tmp/gen --no-install-project --extra matrix'`
3. Check that `/opt/data/cache/uv/.seeded` exists and that no `Building python-olm` line appears.

Existing volume (marker from a seedless image, same lock), `uv pip install python-olm==3.2.16` into a new venv, `--cpus=2`:

| Code | Result |
|---|---|
| `Dockerfile` change only | 43.9 s (`Building python-olm`) |
| plus the `pm/packages.py` change | cache hit, 0.0 s |

`tests/pm/test_uv_cache_seed.py`, `test_uv_cache.py`, `test_uv_cache_publication.py`: 12 passed. A volume that already has a bundle-install marker merges its seed once more on the next call.

Not tested: a real plugin install through PM, and arm64.

## Checklist

- [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) (`fix(scope):`, `feat(scope):`, etc.)

- [ ] I've run `pytest tests/ -q` and all tests pass — I ran `tests/pm/test_uv_cache*.py` (12 passed), CI owns the rest
- [ ] `python scripts/check` passes — not run, CI owns it
- [x] I've added tests for my changes (required for bug fixes, strongly encouraged for features)
- [x] I've tested on my platform: NixOS, Docker, linux/amd64

### Documentation & Housekeeping

prs.title: fix(telegram): let a silence marker stand on group messages not addressed to the bot
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Telegram never set `MessageEvent.reply_expected`, so `silence_allowed()` always saw `None`: a bot told to answer `[SILENT]` to group chatter posted "The model returned only a silence marker…" to the whole group instead. This sets the per-message signal from #123271 on Telegram, with the same rule #133672 gives WhatsApp, plus an opt-in for groups where the bot is meant to decide for itself when to speak.

| Telegram message | `reply_expected` | Bare silence marker |
|---|---|---|
| DM; or a group message that @mentions the bot, replies to it, matches `mention_patterns`, or is a `/command` | `True` | notice (#110952 unchanged) |
| Group: replies to another member, or opens by @mentioning someone else | `False` | stays silent |
| Group: any other message without a `?` | `False` | stays silent |
| Group: any other message with a `?` | `None` | notice: it may be a question for the bot |
| …the same, in a group listed in `telegram.ambient_chats` | `False` | stays silent |
| Channel posts; group messages while the bot's identity is unknown | `None` | notice (as on `main`) |

`telegram.ambient_chats` (chat IDs, `config.yaml` only, empty by default) is the operator's explicit "this bot reads everything and picks when to speak", for groups where most chatter between members is questions. Messages addressed to the bot are still `True` there.

## Related Issue

Part of #120051 (the Telegram case; WhatsApp is #133672, Discord still needs its own adapter change). Approach discussed in https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/120051#issuecomment-6007104567.

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)
- [ ] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality)
- [ ] 🔒 Security fix
- [ ] 📝 Documentation update
- [ ] ✅ Tests (adding or improving test coverage)
- [ ] ♻️ Refactor (no behavior change)
- [ ] 🎯 New skill (bundled or hub)

## Changes Made

- `plugins/platforms/telegram/telegram_context.py`: `group_reply_expected()` next to the existing group-addressing helpers. `starts_with_other_participant_mention()` (leading address) shares its entity and identity checks with `mentions_other_participants()` (anywhere), which keeps its behaviour. A `/command` in a caption counts like one in text; a bot identity without a username gives `None`.
- `plugins/platforms/telegram/telegram_config.py` (new): validates `telegram.ambient_chats` at load. Negative chat IDs as a YAML list, JSON-list string or CSV; anything else raises a `PlatformConfigError` naming the key, instead of a `TypeError` while handling a message.
- `plugins/platforms/telegram/telegram_media.py` (new) and `adapter.py`: photo bursts and albums merge through `absorb_reply_expected`, so a bot-addressed photo arriving after unaddressed ones keeps `True` in either order. `_build_message_event` sets `reply_expected` for every inbound path. `adapter.py` shrinks by 6 lines, so the file-size ratchet holds.
- `gateway/config_loader.py`, `gateway/config.py`: authored adapter keys reach plugin config hooks in both the direct and `extra` spelling, so an unrelated root `telegram:` block no longer hides a nested setting from validation; managed pins keep precedence over user extras in either spelling; config errors propagate instead of being swallowed. This also applies to the Slack and Discord bridges (covered in `test_config_hook_resolution.py`).
- `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py`, `cli-config.yaml.example`: register `telegram.ambient_chats: []`.
- Tests: `test_telegram_reply_expected.py` (captions, identities, mention policy), `test_telegram_media_reply_expected.py` (bursts and albums, both orders), `test_telegram_ambient_config.py` (accepted forms, rejections, profile isolation A→B→A, nested/managed precedence), `test_config_hook_resolution.py`, plus updates to `test_telegram_group_gating.py` and `test_telegram_thread_fallback.py`.
- `website/docs/user-guide/messaging/telegram.md` ("Letting the bot stay silent in a group") and `index.md` (silence tokens): the rule, the setting, its accepted forms and precedence.
- `contributors/emails/diego@sanch.dev`: attribution mapping.

## How to Test

1. `scripts/run_tests.sh tests/gateway/test_telegram_reply_expected.py tests/gateway/test_telegram_media_reply_expected.py tests/gateway/test_telegram_ambient_config.py tests/gateway/test_config_hook_resolution.py tests/gateway/test_telegram_group_gating.py`: each new file was written red first (4 media, 11 addressing, 39 config failures before the fixes).
2. Telegram group with `require_mention: false` and a SOUL that answers `[SILENT]` to chatter. On `main`, every unaddressed message posts the notice. On this branch, plain chatter and a reply to another member stay silent; a question stays silent only with the group in `telegram.ambient_chats`; `@bot …` still gets an answer.

## Checklist

### Code

- [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)
- [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate (#133672 is the WhatsApp half and continues #117223; #117354 takes the per-chat-type route; #112000 is a profile-wide opt-in, DMs included)
- [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix/feature
- [ ] I've run `pytest tests/ -q` and all tests pass: the 16 files this PR touches or depends on: 513 passed, 0 failed, 4 skipped (Windows-only), retries disabled. The wider 102-file Telegram/silence/config set: 1082 passed, 14 failed, all 14 in `tests/e2e/core/platforms/test_telegram_contract.py` because the local test environment lacks `python-telegram-bot` (same 14 fail on `main`). Base `7cc3fb8cb5`; not rerun on the current `main`.
- [x] `python scripts/check` passes (12 checks, code health 0 blocking, 0 advisory)
- [x] I've added tests for my changes
- [x] I've tested on my platform: macOS 27.0.1, live Telegram group via the Hermes gateway (see Screenshots / Logs)

### Documentation & Housekeeping

- [x] I've updated relevant documentation
- [x] I've updated `cli-config.yaml.example` if I added/changed config keys
- [x] I've updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `AGENTS.md` if I changed architecture or workflows: N/A
- [x] I've considered cross-platform impact: N/A, no file I/O, processes or paths
- [x] I've updated tool descriptions/schemas if I changed tool behavior: N/A

## Screenshots / Logs

Before (without this change), in a two-person household group:

```
WARNING gateway.run: silence marker rejected on a user turn: platform=telegram chat=-100…
```

…and the group received "⚠️ The model returned only a silence marker for a message that needed a reply. Try again or rephrase." on an ordinary message between the two members.

After, with this change on the same gateway and the group listed in `ambient_chats`: the bot kept answering the messages it chose to answer, and a plain update posted to the group ended in the bot's `[SILENT]` without anything else appearing:

```
INFO gateway.run: Suppressing intentional silence marker for session 2026…
```

That live check ran the first version of this PR. The reply-to-another-member and question rows were not exercised live, and the batching/validation follow-ups have not been run live yet; the tests cover them.

prs.title: feat(openrouter): configurable in-region endpoints (global/eu/us)
prs.body:
## Summary

OpenRouter's in-region routing (Business/Enterprise) selects the region by **base URL** — `https://us.openrouter.ai/api/v1` / `https://eu.openrouter.ai/api/v1` — not by a request-body flag. Hermes previously hardcoded the global host (`https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`) everywhere, so workspaces whose guardrail restricts keys to `us.openrouter.ai` fail every request with:

```
HTTP 403: This request arrived on the global data region, but the key's workspace permits
requests only on these OpenRouter hostnames: us.openrouter.ai.
```

This adds an `openrouter.endpoint` setting (`global` | `eu` | `us`, default `global` — current behaviour) and threads it through every OpenRouter request path.

## Changes

- **`hermes_constants.py`** — `OPENROUTER_ENDPOINTS` table + `openrouter_endpoint_url()` mapping (accepts `global`/`eu`/`us`, a URL, or a bare regional host; unknown/empty falls back to Global).
- **`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py`** — new `openrouter.endpoint` default key (`"global"`).
- **`hermes_cli/model_setup_flows.py`** — `hermes model` on OpenRouter now prompts for the endpoint before the model picker, showing each URL and the Business+ note, and persists the choice to both `openrouter.endpoint` and `model.base_url`.
- **`hermes_cli/runtime_provider_backends.py`** — the OpenRouter/custom fallback resolver applies `openrouter.endpoint` when `model.base_url` is an official OpenRouter host (or unset); custom mirrors/proxies are never rewritten.
- **`hermes_cli/runtime_provider.py`** — the credential-pool path: env-seeded pool rows are stamped with the global host and win the credential ladder *before* the fallback resolver, so `_pool_entry_mode_and_url` rewrites official hosts the same way. This was the path the 403 actually came from in live use.
- **`agent/auxiliary_client.py`** — auxiliary OpenRouter clients (title generation, compression, vision, …) follow the endpoint too; a caller-supplied `explicit_base_url` (fallback_providers / custom_providers) stays authoritative per #121359.
- **`website/docs/integrations/providers.md`** — new "OpenRouter in-region endpoints" section with the endpoint table and YAML example.

## Behaviour

| `openrouter.endpoint` | Base URL | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `global` (default) | `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1` | unchanged |
| `eu` | `https://eu.openrouter.ai/api/v1` | requires Business+ plan |
| `us` | `https://us.openrouter.ai/api/v1` | requires Business+ plan |

- A `model.base_url` that is NOT one of the three official hosts (proxy/mirror) is never touched.
- If no in-region provider can serve the model, OpenRouter returns 404 rather than leaving the region.

## Test plan

- [x] `tests/hermes_cli/test_runtime_provider_resolution.py -k openrouter` — 22 passed
- [x] `tests/agent/test_auxiliary_client.py -k openrouter` — no new failures vs. baseline (8 pre-existing environment failures on this checkout, identical with the change stashed)
- [x] Manual: with `openrouter.endpoint: us`, resolver, pool entry, and auxiliary clients all resolve `https://us.openrouter.ai/api/v1`; custom mirror URLs pass through untouched
- [x] Live: 403 gone against a US-only workspace guardrail

Verified live end-to-end on a US-only OpenRouter workspace (main agent, credential-pool rows, and title generation all arriving on `us.openrouter.ai`).

prs.title: fix(transports): strip the `message_id` replay alias from outgoing messages
prs.body:
## What

Strip the `message_id` replay alias from every outgoing message, exactly where its sibling `platform_message_id` is already stripped.

## Why

`hermes_state_messages._rows_to_conversation` re-exposes the durable `messages.platform_message_id` column under the JSONL-transcript name `message_id`, so a replayed gateway turn carries **both** keys. Every strip list drops `platform_message_id`; the alias was missed and reached the wire.

A strict Chat Completions schema rejects the whole request — Fireworks' `ChatMessage` is `additionalProperties: false`:

```
HTTP 400: 2 request validation errors: Extra inputs are not permitted,
field: 'messages[1].message_id', value: '7515969557947007112';
Extra inputs are not permitted, field: 'messages[11].message_id', value: '7515970189638607240'
```

The error is non-retryable, and since the offending rows stay in context it repeats on **every** turn of that conversation. In practice a Weixin/gateway conversation whose history carries a platform message id could not call such a model at all.

## How

The alias is now treated like its sibling in all three places the sibling is handled:

- `PERSISTENCE_ONLY_MESSAGE_FIELDS` — `turn_context` pops this set from every outgoing copy (the summary path ORs the set in, so it is covered too).
- `chat_completions._STRIP_MSG_KEYS` — the transport sweeps its own tuple.
- `chat_completion_helpers._SUMMARY_FOREIGN_MESSAGE_KEYS` — kept explicit so the three lists stay auditable side by side.

Durable rows keep `platform_message_id` (`session_persistence` / `_rows_to_conversation` read the live dict), so persistence and JSONL export are unaffected.

## Verification

Against the live failing request (a real 76-message body Fireworks had rejected):

| payload | result |
|---|---|
| replayed as-is | `HTTP 400` — identical error text |
| after `ChatCompletionsTransport.convert_messages()` | `HTTP 200` |

`message_id` disappears from `messages[1]` and `messages[11]`; no other key changes (a clean history is returned by identity, so the prompt-cache prefix is untouched).

Two regression tests are added — `tests/agent/transports/test_chat_completions.py::TestChatCompletionsBasic::test_convert_messages_strips_platform_message_id_alias` and `tests/agent/test_message_metadata.py::test_without_persistence_fields_drops_platform_message_id_alias`. Both fail on the pre-fix tree with the alias still present and pass with the fix:

```
$ pytest tests/agent/test_message_metadata.py tests/agent/transports/test_chat_completions.py -q
60 passed
```

prs.title: fix(vault): pass --vault on 1Password item get for service accounts and support schemeless URLs
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Fixes two issues with the 1Password vault backend when running with service account authentication or items having schemeless URLs:

1. **Service Account item resolution**: When `op` is authenticated via a Service Account (`OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN`), `op item get <item_id>` fails if `--vault` is not explicitly provided. This change extracts and encodes the `vault_id` into the handle (`op:<vault_id>/<item_id>`) during `list_items()`, caches it in `_VAULT_CACHE`, and passes `--vault <vault_id>` during `resolve_password()` and `resolve_otp()`. Bare handles (`op:<item_id>`) retain backwards compatibility via lazy cache resolution or fallback config.
2. **Schemeless URL origin normalization**: Items saved in 1Password with bare domain URLs (e.g., `example.com` rather than `https://example.com`) were previously skipped by `list_items()` because `urllib.parse.urlparse` parses them with empty `netloc`. Schemeless URLs now default to `https://` during origin extraction so they match page origins correctly.

prs.title: fix(gateway): spawn the updater in its own systemd transient unit
prs.body:
## Problem

The `/update` command spawns the updater with `setsid`, which detaches the **session** but leaves the process **inside the gateway's systemd cgroup**. A gateway restart — which the update itself triggers at the end, and which external watchers (e.g. a code-skew heal timer) may also issue mid-run — SIGKILLs the entire cgroup (`KillMode=mixed`), destroying the updater and its bash wrapper mid-build. The update is stranded with no exit code, a stale lock, and a 30-minute spurious timeout.

## Fix

When a systemd user manager is reachable, spawn the updater as a **transient systemd user unit** (`systemd-run --user --collect --unit=hermes-update-<pid>-<ts> bash -c …`) so it runs in **its own cgroup** and survives gateway restarts.

- Probe the user manager first with a bounded `systemd-run … true` call (5s timeout) so we never silently fail to start the update.
- Fall back to the existing `setsid` spawn, then to `start_new_session=True`, when `systemd-run` is missing or no user session is reachable (the original reason `setsid` was chosen — e.g. the gateway running as a root system service without a user bus).
- Windows path untouched.

## Why this approach

- This is the **structural** fix: the updater can no longer be killed by a gateway restart at all, instead of only being detected afterwards.
- Conservative fallback chain: on any systemd failure, behavior is identical to today.
- `--collect` garbage-collects the transient unit after exit; the unit name is unique per spawn.

## Validation

- New unit tests in `tests/gateway/test_update_command.py`:
  - `systemd-run` available + probe OK → Popen called with `systemd-run --user --collect` and the update command
  - probe fails → falls back to the `setsid` spawn (no silent failure)
- Existing spawn tests unchanged and passing (`test_spawns_with_gateway_flag`, `test_writes_pending_marker`, `test_fallback_when_no_setsid`, …) — 17 passed in `tests/gateway/test_update_command.py`.

prs.title: fix(checkpoints): recover from stale git locks in the shadow store
prs.body:
## Problem

A git process killed mid-write (gateway restart with `KillMode=mixed`, crash, OOM) leaves its `<target>.lock` file behind in the checkpoint shadow store. Every later git command needing that target then fails with:

```
fatal: Unable to create '.../checkpoints/store/indexes/<hash>.lock': File exists.
```

(rc=128) until a human removes the file by hand. The checkpoint manager has no recovery for this — it silently returns `False` from `_take()` and the affected project never gets snapshots again.

### Reproduction (production, Aug 2026)

Two abandoned locks sat in the store since **2026-08-04** and **2026-08-13** (killed git processes — no live process can hold a lock for that long). From that point on, every checkpoint snapshot of the affected project failed identically, 18+ times in a 24h window:

```
ERROR tools.checkpoint_manager: Git command failed: git add -A (rc=128)
  stderr=fatal: Unable to create '.../indexes/e9671acd244849c5.lock': File exists.
```

Manual repro of the same failure:

```
$ GIT_DIR=.../checkpoints/store GIT_INDEX_FILE=.../indexes/e9671acd244849c5 git add -A
fatal: Unable to create '.../indexes/e9671acd244849c5.lock': File exists.
```

Git itself suggests "remove the file manually to continue" — exactly what the manager should do, safely, on its own.

## Fix

- **`_repair_stale_locks(store)`** — sweeps the store for `.lock` files older than `_STALE_LOCK_MAX_AGE_S` (600s) and unlinks them. Git holds a lock for the duration of a single command bounded by `_GIT_TIMEOUT` (30s), so anything older is abandoned by definition; a live concurrent git process is never disturbed (10-minute margin).
- **`_run_git` retry** — on the exact failure signature (rc=128 + `Unable to create` + `File exists`), run the sweep and retry the command once. This covers every call site (snapshot, diff, restore, prune) in one place.
- **`_init_store` proactive sweep** — the shared entry point of every snapshot path clears stale locks before any git command runs, so the first operation never fails.

Why a bounded retry instead of always sweeping before every git call: sweeping is only needed when a lock is actually present, and the retry makes the repair self-healing at the exact point of failure while the proactive sweep keeps the common path clean.

## Validation

- 3 new regression tests in `tests/tools/test_checkpoint_manager.py`:
  - `test_repair_only_removes_old_locks` — fresh lock kept, stale lock removed, count correct
  - `test_run_git_retries_once_after_clearing_stale_lock` — the exact production failure (stale lock on the per-project index) now succeeds via the retry path
  - `test_snapshot_succeeds_after_stale_lock_repair` — end-to-end through `ensure_checkpoint`
- Full file suite: **47 passed** (3 failures in `TestSafeRestore` are pre-existing on `main` — verified by stashing the change and re-running; unrelated safe-restore user-edit tests)
- `ruff check` clean on both changed files
- Production observation: after the fix removed the two abandoned locks, the previously failing `git add -A` for the affected project succeeds

prs.title: fix(desktop): opening a non-active-profile session leaves its unread dot
prs.body:
## Problem

A session in a **non-active profile** that finishes a turn in the background keeps its green "finished — unread" dot even after the user opens it. The dot only clears if the profile's section is re-loaded (so the row is present for the ack) or the session is **unpinned** (which drops it from the loaded scope — a data-hiding side effect, not a read).

Repro (observed with a pinned session from a second profile while the gateway was on the default profile):

1. A turn finishes in the background for a session owned by profile `alpha` while the active gateway profile is `default`. The live edge (`markSessionUnreadFinished`) persists the marker under **the row's own profile** — `alpha` — by design (markers are profile-scoped; session ids are per-profile namespaces).
2. The `alpha` section unloads (scope switch / collapsed profile) so no matching row is loaded.
3. The user opens the session. `ackStoredSessionId` hits its no-row fallback, which retires the marker **only from the active gateway's bucket** (`default`).
4. The marker survives in `alpha`, and `recomputeUnread` re-paints the dot on the next list refresh — for as long as the row is visible again.

## Fix

`ackStoredSessionId`'s no-row fallback now adapts to the `profileHint` design on `main` (rework of the original sweep, 2026-09-14):

- A caller-supplied `profileHint` still scopes the ack to **that bucket only** (falling back to the active gateway's) — hidden sessions (Bot Mode canonical chats) stay precise and other profiles' identically-named ids stay untouched.
- A loaded row still acks via `ackSessionRow`, resolving the profile from the row itself (unchanged) — same-id sessions in different profiles remain independent.
- When **no row and no hint** resolve, the ack retires the marker from **every** bucket. This is the case that carries the bug: the store's own listeners (`$selectedStoredSessionId.listen`, `$focusedStoredSessionId.listen`) have no owner to hint with, and the live edge filed the marker under the ROW's own profile — any profile, not just the active gateway's. The user opened this id, so it is seen now; the row path above keeps same-id sessions independent whenever rows are loaded, so this fallback cannot silence a gap it wasn't asked about.

## Validation

- New regression test: a marker filed under a non-active profile is acked when the row is not loaded, and a later list refresh does not repaint the dot. **Fails against current `main`** (marker survives the ack) — RED/GREEN proven by reverting the one-hunk source change.
- New hint-scoping test: a hinted no-row ack touches only the hinted bucket.
- `session-unread.test.ts` 16/16, `session-unread-remote.test.ts` 8/8, `session-states.test.ts` (hosts the selection/focus listeners) 81/81 — vitest `--project ui`.
- `eslint` clean on both changed files; desktop `tsc -p . --noEmit` passes.

prs.title: fix(file-sync): skip permission-denied host files instead of wedging the sync cycle
prs.body:
## Problem

A single host file that cannot be read (upload direction) or cannot be written (sync-back direction) wedged the whole file-sync pipeline:

- **Upload:** the unreadable file fails the transactional cycle; state rolls back and the rate-limit clock never advances, so every subsequent sync retries the full set and nothing else ever reaches the remote.
- **Sync-back:** applying the remote tar raised `PermissionError` on the unwritable host path, failing the transaction; the retry re-ran the full file set, so every other remote change stayed blocked behind it — `sync_back: attempt N failed …` / `all attempts failed` warnings on every cycle.

Both are reachable in normal operation — e.g. a read-only (mode 444) file left behind under `~/.hermes/skills/.archive/…`: on a production install this produced ~60 warning lines/day across sessions, with sync-back never converging.

## Fix

- `_plan_sync` skips host files that are not readable (`os.access(..., R_OK)`) with a one-time warning; re-checked every cycle, picked up automatically once readable.
- `_apply_staged_file` skips host paths whose write fails (`OSError`) with a one-time warning; retried automatically once writable.
- Skip-bookkeeping sets are pruned to the current file set so entries do not accumulate.
- Tests: unreadable/no-wedge + automatic recovery (upload), unwritable/no-crash + others-still-apply + no duplicate warning (sync-back).

## Validation

- `scripts/run_tests.sh tests/tools/test_file_sync.py` — **19/19 passed** on the branch head.
- **Red on base:** the four coverage tests fail on current `main` (same file) with meaningful assertions, e.g. `assert '/root/.hermes/skill_main.py' not in {…, '/root/.hermes/skill_main.py'}` — then pass on the branch head.
- Refreshed and rebased onto current `main` (`b6b53c69`); the file_sync refactor-era staged-paths interface is accounted for (`_plan_sync` extraction, transport receives staged copies — tests assert on stable remote paths).

prs.title: fix(gateway): refuse inbound turns on stale code instead of ImportError crash
prs.body:
fix(gateway): refuse inbound turns on stale code instead of ImportError crash

A long-lived gateway/serve process holds `sys.modules` from boot. When
`hermes update` (or a manual `git pull`) replaces the checkout underneath
it but the unit is not restarted — e.g. root-gated systemd restart of
`hermes-serve` is skipped and left to the operator — the first inbound
message on a new code path lazily imports a freshly-pulled consumer module
against the stale boot-time module graph and crashes with a cryptic
`cannot import name ...` (observed in production:

    cannot import name 'fill_empty_non_final_wire_payload'
    from 'agent.agent_runtime_helpers'

on a serve process kept alive across an update). The desktop shows a
"Gateway error" banner and the user's message is lost.

The codebase already guards the two highest-risk import sites with the
shared detector in `gateway/code_skew.py`:
- model switching (`_model_switch_skew_guard`, slash_commands.py, #97046)
- the dashboard model picker (`_dashboard_code_skew_guard`,
  web_server.py, #86207)

The plain-message turn path — the first lazy-import site a stale process
actually hits — was still unguarded ("we don't guard every import site,
only this one"). This adds the mirror guard for turns:

- `GatewayRunner._turn_code_skew_guard()` returns a deployment-agnostic
  "restart the backend" notice when `detect_code_skew()` reports drift
  (never a false positive: no boot fingerprint -> no refusal).
- `_handle_message_with_agent` checks it before any session/agent work and
  refuses with the notice delivered via `_deliver_platform_notice`
  (platform privacy rules respected) instead of crashing. The user's
  message is not silently lost; they are told to restart and resend.

Why not restart automatically: the serve unit restart is often root-gated
(polkit/sudo), which is exactly the case that leaves the stale process
running; the update already surfaces "restart manually" guidance. The
guard makes the failure mode a clear instruction instead of a crash.

Tests: three additions to tests/test_code_skew.py — guard returns None
without skew, message names both revisions and the restart action without
hardcoding a systemd unit, and a behavioral test proving a skewed handler
delivers the notice and never spawns the agent.

Validation: tests/test_code_skew.py (15 passed) and
tests/test_stale_utils_module_import.py (3 passed) with the project venv;
ruff clean.

prs.title: fix(gateway): suppress emphasis-wrapped silence markers in the autonomous lane
prs.body:
## Symptom

A cron job whose agent ended its turn with `**[SILENT]**` had that literal text delivered to the user's Telegram chat — a marker-only message the user then asked about. The same turn's work had concluded "nothing needs the owner", i.e. the run *intended* silence.

Reproduced live on 2026-09-13 04:09 UTC:

```
2026-09-13 04:08:10 INFO __main__: Job 'Daily agent-file integrity watchdog' completed successfully
2026-09-13 04:09:10 INFO cron.scheduler: Job 'ec3a8cad9ef5': delivered to telegram:... message_id=14880
```

with the turn's final response being exactly `**[SILENT]**` (12 chars, `response_len=12` in the same log).

## Where it manifests

`gateway/response_filters.py` → `is_autonomous_silence_response()` (the loose matcher used by the cron and webhook lanes; `cron/scheduler.py::_is_cron_silence_response` is a thin delegate, and `cron/scheduler.py` gates delivery on it).

The matcher canonicalizes its three candidates with `_canonical_silence_candidate()` (singular), which only `.strip().upper()`s and collapses whitespace. It never calls `_canonical_silence_candidates()` (plural) — the one helper that runs `_strip_edge_silence_punctuation()` — so `**[SILENT]**` canonicalizes to `**[SILENT]**` and misses `LIVE_GATEWAY_SILENT_MARKERS`.

The sibling lane already handles it: `is_intentional_silence_response()` iterates the *plural* candidates, so `**[SILENT]**` suppresses on the interactive path. The two lanes therefore diverge by accident, not by design.

## Fix

Reuse the existing plural helper at every candidate position, and strip edge punctuation for the bracketed prefix rule too (so `**[SILENT]** No changes detected` behaves like `[SILENT] No changes detected`). Deliberate guards are preserved:

- a marker buried mid-sentence still delivers (`we should send [SILENT] at the end`)
- prose that merely mentions a marker still delivers (`The reply was [SILENT], intentionally.`)
- a blank response is still the empty-response failure path, not silence
- `[]` stays structural, so a malformed `[SILENT` cannot become `SILENT`

## Tests

One invariant test added to `tests/gateway/test_response_filters.py`: `test_autonomous_silence_accepts_emphasis_wrapped_marker`.

RED on the unpatched base (`scripts/run_tests.sh tests/gateway/test_response_filters.py`):

```
tests/gateway/test_response_filters.py ..F                               [100%]
>       assert is_autonomous_silence_response("**[SILENT]**")
E       AssertionError: assert False
FAILED tests/gateway/test_response_filters.py::test_autonomous_silence_accepts_emphasis_wrapped_marker
========================= 1 failed, 2 passed in 6.85s ==========================
```

GREEN with the fix (`scripts/run_tests.sh tests/gateway/test_response_filters.py tests/gateway/test_gateway_silence_tokens.py tests/gateway/test_stream_consumer_silence.py tests/gateway/test_delivery_silence_filter.py tests/cron/test_scheduler.py`):

```
=== Summary: 5 files, 138 tests passed, 0 failed (100% complete) in 37.0s (4 workers) ===
```

prs.title: fix(agent): guard the sequential tool submit against interpreter shutdown
prs.body:
## Problem

A tool call that is still being *scheduled* when the interpreter begins finalizing hits CPython's module-global shutdown flag and `DaemonThreadPoolExecutor.submit` raises:

```
RuntimeError: cannot schedule new futures after interpreter shutdown
```

In the sequential tool path this RuntimeError propagates out of `_run_sequential_tool_execution_middleware` (`agent/tool_executor.py:857` → `tools/daemon_pool.py:36`), and surfaces as an ERROR with a full traceback per tool call during teardown:

```
agent.tool_executor: handle_function_call raised for terminal: cannot schedule new futures after interpreter shutdown
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../agent/tool_executor.py", line 1594, in _run_sequential_call
    managed = _run_sequential_tool_execution_middleware(
  File ".../agent/tool_executor.py", line 857, in _run_sequential_tool_execution_middleware
    future = executor.submit(propagate_context_to_thread(_run))
RuntimeError: cannot schedule new futures after interpreter shutdown
```

Measured on the reporting host (one gateway, error logs Sep 12–14): **83 occurrences across 7 distinct sessions**, every one traced through that single submit site — the last unguarded tool-submission site of its class.

## Reproduction

Patch `DaemonThreadPoolExecutor.submit` to raise the exact CPython error and call the middleware the way `_run_sequential_call` does (scratch checkout at current `main`):

```
$ python repro.py
PROPAGATED RuntimeError: cannot schedule new futures after interpreter shutdown
    File ".../agent/tool_executor.py", line 857, in _run_sequential_tool_execution_middleware
RuntimeError: cannot schedule new futures after interpreter shutdown
```

With this branch, same repro:

```
SYNTHESIZED: _ToolShutdownResult | Error executing tool 'read_file': Python interpreter is shutting down; tool was not started
```

## Fix

The concurrent batch path already converts unsubmitted slots into per-call error results from the same signal — `_ConcurrentBatch.submit_all` routes through the shared `tools.interpreter_shutdown` predicate, whose docstring names this exact bug class (#55924/#58720) and says **all** submit sites should recognize both CPython message variants. The sequential path never got that treatment; this branch mirrors it:

- Wrap the `submit`; re-raise any RuntimeError the shared predicate does not recognize, so a genuine broken pool still surfaces.
- No worker was started, so synthesize the sibling `_ToolShutdownResult` marker with the concurrent path's exact message (`... Python interpreter is shutting down; tool was not started`), emit the single terminal `post_tool_call` (`status=error`, `error_type=interpreter_shutdown`), and fold the marker into `_publish_sequential_result`'s synthesized-result handling so no second hook fires and effect accounting stays conservative.

**Why not guard inside `daemon_pool.submit` itself:** synthesis needs the tool-call context (ref/name/args) to produce the per-call result and terminal hook; `DaemonThreadPoolExecutor` is shared infrastructure (relay scope ops, memory sync) where silently swallowing scheduling errors would change semantics.

**Why not only at the caller's `except` in `_run_sequential_call`:** that route converts only dispatches carrying `error_result` and still logs ERROR + traceback; handling at the submit site fixes both that route and the raising route with one behavior, matching the concurrent side.

## Validation

- New `tests/agent/test_sequential_tool_interpreter_shutdown.py`: both CPython message variants (`...after interpreter shutdown` / `...after shutdown`) synthesize the marker result with exactly one hook; a non-shutdown `RuntimeError("broken pool")` still propagates. Red→green: on unfixed `main` the repro raises through `tool_executor.py:857`; on the branch it synthesizes.
- Focused set — `scripts/run_tests.sh tests/agent/test_sequential_tool_interpreter_shutdown.py tests/agent/test_sequential_tool_interrupt.py tests/agent/test_interpreter_shutdown_turn_exit.py tests/agent/test_conversation_loop_interpreter_shutdown.py` → **4 files, 23 tests passed, 0 failed**.
- Blast-radius sweep over the surrounding executor machinery (sequential timeout / deadline-exempt delegate / start-order gate / authorization gate / checkpoint paths / activity heartbeat / batch segmentation / malformed args / incremental persistence / deadline): **10 files, 149 tests passed, 1 skipped (windows-only lane)** — 0 failures.

prs.title: docs(cli): document the six undocumented hermes update flags
prs.body:
## Problem

`website/docs/reference/cli-commands.md` documents only 6 of the 12 flags `hermes update` actually accepts:

```
hermes update [--gateway] [--check] [--plan] [--no-backup] [--backup] [--yes]
```

**Reproduction:** run `hermes update --help` (or read `hermes_cli/subcommands/update.py` on current main) — the parser registers `--keep-stash`, `--branch`, `--switch-branch`, `--no-gateway-restart`, `--force`, and `--force-venv` in addition to the six documented flags. All six undocumented flags are real, shipped behavior: `--no-gateway-restart` is the documented cron/automation path (already covered in prose on `website/docs/getting-started/updating.md` §"Automated updates from inside the gateway"), `--keep-stash` is what the desktop updater invokes, and the two Windows guards (`--force`/`--force-venv`) are the only way to proceed past concurrent-process detection.

## Fix

- Extend the usage synopsis to the full flag set.
- Add a row for each missing flag to the `hermes update` option table, with descriptions matching the parser help and the existing prose pages.

This is documentation-only; no behavior changes.

## Why not an alternative

The prose guide already documents these flags, so the reference page is the one stale surface. Rewriting the guide would duplicate content; a "see also" pointer alone would leave the canonical flag table incomplete for anyone using the reference as the authoritative CLI surface.

## Validation

- Every flag added to the table exists verbatim as an `add_argument` in `hermes_cli/subcommands/update.py` (lines 13–75); after this change the table covers every flag the parser registers (checked programmatically: no `add_argument` flag missing, no table row naming a flag the parser lacks).
- Flag descriptions cross-checked against `hermes_cli/subcommands/update.py` help strings and `website/docs/getting-started/updating.md`.
- Markdown table integrity: all edited rows keep the 3-pipe 2-column shape of the surrounding table.

Problem

A downloaded-but-excluded GGUF or a reused-PID stale server.json makes

- Validates the server.json record against the live listener.

prs.title: fix(auth): surface elapsed state on Nous device-code timeout (#98682)
prs.body:
# Problem

#98682 (pain-miner cluster: "Nous Portal OAuth flows dead-end after sign-in ... with zero client-side error") asks, in its hermes-agent half, that **when device-code polling expires the timeout surface an explicit error with the elapsed state** — not just a bare "timed out".

The Nous device-code timeout message (`hermes_cli/auth_device_flow.py::_nous_device_auth_timeout_message`) already carries the actionable guidance added for #20605 (Portal sign-in required, CAPTCHA hint, `hermes portal` retry, Portal login URL), and the web dashboard surface (`OAuthLoginModal.sessionExpiredNoError`) already names the cause and the fallback. But the CLI/dashboard-poller timeout message still says nothing about **how long the flow waited** — the one piece of elapsed state the issue explicitly asks for. A user watching a 10-minute device-code window expire gets no sense of the wait, and the dashboard poller (`web_server_oauth._nous_promotion_poller`, which surfaces `str(e)` to the UI) inherits the same gap.

# Fix

- `_nous_device_auth_timeout_message(portal_base_url, expires_in=None)` now prepends the elapsed state when the device-code validity window is known: `The device code expired after {n}s without approval.`
- `_poll_for_token` passes its `expires_in` (the device-code response's validity window, which the poll loop waits out before raising) into the timeout factory, so the CLI login and the dashboard poller both inherit the elapsed state at the source.
- When `expires_in` is unknown the line is omitted — no fabricated number.

The existing actionable guidance (CAPTCHA hint, `hermes portal` retry, Portal login URL) is unchanged, so the #20605 behavior is preserved.

# Why not alternatives

- **Not adding the issue's proposed `hermes auth login --api-key` fallback**: that command does not exist (`hermes auth add <provider> --api-key` is the real form), and the Nous provider is `oauth_device_code` — it does not accept API-key credentials at all. Printing a nonexistent command would be worse than the current guidance.
- **Not touching the Desktop native sign-in timeout**: that surface already raises an explicit error with a retry path, and validating an Electron change here would require the desktop toolchain; this PR stays on the Python surface the issue names first ("device-code polling expires").
- **Not changing the loopback PKCE timeout**: that path serves third-party providers (Spotify, Codex, out-of-tree plugins), not the Nous Portal flow this issue covers.

# Validation

- New unit tests in `tests/hermes_cli/test_auth_nous_provider.py`:
  - `test_timeout_message_surfaces_elapsed_state` — `expires_in=600` → "expired after 600s" plus the existing guidance intact.
  - `test_timeout_message_omits_elapsed_when_unknown` — no `expires_in` → no fabricated number.
  - `test_poll_for_token_timeout_raises_actionable_message` extended to assert the elapsed state propagates through `_poll_for_token` (the source both the CLI login and the dashboard poller read).
- `scripts/run_tests.sh` on all 10 test files touching this module: **138 tests passed, 0 failed** (test_auth_nous_provider, test_anon_sign_in_flow, test_ux_messages_auth_config, test_auth_codex_browser_login, test_oauth_pkce_plugin, test_subscription_cli, test_billing_scope_stepup, test_anon_surfaces, test_auth_loopback_ssh_hint, test_login_cli_command, test_web_oauth_dispatch).
- `py_compile` and `ruff check` clean on both changed files.

Addresses part of #98682 (the client-side error-surface half; the Portal-side `callbackUrl` regression and the device-flow approval page remain tracked there and in #47950).
