prs.title: fix(tunnel): supervise and verify the tailscale gateway serve process
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - The gateway's `tailscale serve|funnel --https=443` child was spawned in `TailscaleTunnel::start()` and never waited for. When it exited (port 443 still held by another foreground session, or a lost serve-config etag race with the `--tcp` forwarders started right after it), it stayed `<defunct>` for the life of the daemon. `health_check` still reported it alive because `tokio::process::Child::id()` stays `Some` until the child is polled to completion, and `start()` had already advertised a URL that nothing served.
  - The gateway serve process is now owned by the same watcher the TCP forwarders already use (`TcpForwarder` generalised to `ServeProcess`). An exit is reaped and logged with its stderr, stop or drop kills and reaps it, and `health_check` reflects the real state.
  - `start()` returns the URL only once `tailscale serve status --json` shows a new foreground session proxying `443` to `http://127.0.0.1:<local_port>`. Otherwise it fails with the process's stderr, and the gateway's existing `Err` path falls back to local-only.
  - `listener already exists for port N` (observed on Tailscale 1.104.1) is now retryable alongside the existing etag-conflict case, bounded to five attempts (about 2.5s of linear backoff). A previous generation's session being torn down across a reload is waited out; a holder that stays is reported, not spun on.
  - Serve stdout (an unread banner) is discarded instead of piped, so it can never fill a pipe and block the process.
- **Scope boundary:** No other tunnel provider, no change to the `Tunnel` trait or the gateway crate, no automatic respawn of an exited serve process, and no public exposure change (WSS/enrollment stay tailnet-only). Serve processes orphaned by a daemon that dies without running destructors (crash, SIGKILL) are **not** addressed here: they keep holding the port, and with this PR the next start reports that clearly instead of going defunct. A parent-death signal needs a dedicated spawner thread (Linux `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` is per forking thread, and tokio's `block_in_place` can retire such a thread), so it is left for a separate change.
- **Blast radius:** Tailscale tunnel users only. Behaviour change: if 443 cannot be published, `start()` now fails, so the gateway takes its existing "Tunnel failed to start, falling back to local-only" path and does not go on to publish WSS/enrollment via `publish_tcp_services`. Before, those were published next to a dead 443 proxy. Gateway startup may also wait up to about 2.5s (retries) or 5s (apply timeout) per serve process when tailscaled is slow or the port is held.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11530, Related #11531

### What this does, simply

With the Tailscale tunnel, ZeroClaw starts a `tailscale serve` process to put the gateway on the tailnet at `https://<node>`. If that process failed right away, for example because the port was still in use, ZeroClaw never noticed. The dead process lingered as a "defunct" entry in `ps`, health checks said all was well, and the startup output printed a URL that didn't work. This PR has ZeroClaw watch that process the same way it already watches the WSS/enrollment forwarders. It confirms that Tailscale is actually serving the gateway before printing the URL, waits briefly for a port that is still being released, cleans up the process if it exits, and logs why. It does not restart a process that dies later, and it does not yet clean up serve processes left behind by a daemon that crashed.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `Yes`
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `cli` (`zeroclaw daemon` with `[tunnel] tunnel_provider = "tailscale"`)
- **Setup / preconditions:** Linux node logged into a tailnet (`tailscale up`), serve permitted for the operator (`tailscale set --operator=$USER`), `[tunnel] tunnel_provider = "tailscale"`.
- **Steps to run:**
  1. In another terminal, hold the gateway port: `tailscale serve --https=443 8080` (leave it running).
  2. Start `zeroclaw daemon`.
  3. `ps -eo pid,stat,cmd | grep 'tailscale serve'`
  4. Stop the holder from step 1 and restart the daemon.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** Step 2 prints `Tunnel failed to start: tailscale serve --https=443 <port> did not publish the gateway: exited (exit status: 1) after 5 attempt(s): ... listener already exists for port 443` and falls back to local-only. Step 3 shows no `<defunct>` entry. After step 4, `Tunnel active: https://<node>` and `tailscale serve status` shows the gateway proxy.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** Step 2 prints `Tunnel active: https://<node>` even though nothing serves it, and step 3 shows `tailscale serve --https=443 <port> <defunct>` for as long as the daemon runs.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** The CI `Clippy` job (`scripts/ci/run_clippy.sh --scope workspace`, Rust 1.98.0, `--features ci-all`, `-D warnings`) and the test jobs cover the changed Rust file. I ran the same clippy script locally on this head as well (below).
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** No CI job runs a real `tailscaled`. tailscaled's behaviour is pinned by the manual check below, and the tests use `sh` stand-ins for the process plus status JSON captured from a live 1.104.1 node.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```sh
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
# clean (no diff)

$ RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=1.98.0 RUNNER_TEMP=$PWD/target/ci-tmp \
    bash scripts/ci/run_clippy.sh --scope workspace --summary-title "Lint diagnostics" --log-name cargo-clippy.log
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 3m 20s
# exit 0; 0 warning/error lines in cargo-clippy.log

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib tunnel::
test tunnel::tailscale::tests::gateway_serve_exit_is_reaped_not_left_defunct ... ok
test tunnel::tailscale::tests::dropping_the_tunnel_kills_and_reaps_its_gateway_serve ... ok
test tunnel::tailscale::tests::gateway_sessions_match_only_an_https_proxy_to_the_local_port ... ok
test tunnel::tailscale::tests::held_port_is_retryable_but_other_failures_are_not ... ok
```

prs.title: fix(runtime): deliver mid-turn steering at the next step, not after the final answer
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - A message sent with `session/steer` while the agent was working through tool calls only reached the model after the agent had given its final answer. If the turn was cancelled first, the message was lost. The streamed Agent turn ran each round's tool loop with `steering: None` and drained steering only before a round and after the loop returned its final text.
  - The tool loop now receives the steering receiver, together with a new `LoopKnobs::yield_to_steering`. After a tool round, if a message is waiting, the loop stops with `SteeringPending` and does not drain the message itself.
  - The wrapper commits that round's text, then handles the steering through the same `prepare_steering` / `readmit_prepared_steering` path it already uses at the end of a round. The memory write, the sender re-check and the steered round's tool ceiling from #11132 all still apply. The steered round continues the same turn.
- **Scope boundary:** Only the streamed Agent turn changes. The knob defaults to `false`, so other loop callers keep draining inside the loop as before. No change to the RPC or wire format, no new setting. Steering is still read between steps, so a single long tool call isn't interrupted.
- **Blast radius:** Every streamed turn that has a steering receiver: RPC `session/steer`, the gateway chat socket and ACP. Turns with no steering waiting behave exactly as before.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11132, Related #11621

### What this does, simply

When you send a message while the agent is busy, it now sees the message at its next step, right after the tool it's running finishes. Before, it only saw the message after it had already written its final answer.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface`: `tui` (with #11621), or any `session/steer` client
- **Setup / preconditions:** A daemon from this branch, and zerocode from #11621.
- **Steps to run:** Start a prompt that runs several tool calls one after another. While it's working, send "also say hello" and press Enter.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The agent responds to the message at its next tool step, still within the same turn.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** The agent carries on with its tool calls and only gets the message after writing its final answer. If you cancel before then, the message is lost.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `CI Required Gate` (fmt, clippy, workspace tests) covers `zeroclaw-runtime`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** No end-to-end test against a live daemon.
- **Commands run and tail output:** All via the remote cargo wrapper.
  - `cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- steer` → `test result: ok. 29 passed; 0 failed`. This includes the new `steering_sent_during_a_tool_reaches_the_next_step`: a tool sends a steer while it runs, and the test checks that the model's next call sees it after the tool's result, with the message persisted once.
  - Mutation check: with `steering: None` restored in the streamed turn, the new test fails (`FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed`).
  - `cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib` → `5712 passed; 4 failed`. Three of the failures (`relay::local_dial_tests::a_closed_route_releases_a_dial_parked_on_a_stalled_listener`, `relay::local_dial_tests::a_dial_that_never_connects_ends_on_its_own_budget` and `rpc::dispatch::tests::new_session_methods_are_denied_without_their_grants`) fail the same way on unmodified `master` `f12da7462a`. The fourth, `peer_turn_cost_scope_through_execute_boundary_attributes_recipient_and_shares_budget`, passed when rerun alone on this branch and passes on master, so it looks flaky.
  - `cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings` → exit 0.
  - `rustfmt --check` on the changed files and `scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh` both pass.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** I hit the bug live: a steer sent during three tool rounds never reached the model, and cancelling dropped it. With the fix in the experiment build ([experiment/zerocode-builds/20261014T024640Z-eb55856696a7](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/tree/experiment/zerocode-builds/20261014T024640Z-eb55856696a7), commit [eb55856696a7](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/commit/eb55856696a7), dogfood base [0341618f9d69](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/commit/0341618f9d69e31bf38300d134ba86e98491d49d)) and #11621's client, I sent a message while the agent was running tool calls. It reached the agent at the next tool step, within the same turn.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A, no UI change.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** head of this branch; unit tests.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** See the tests above.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** None.

prs.title: feat(memory): stamp recalled entries with their storage date
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - `render_memory_context` renders each recalled entry as `- {key}: {content}`. The key is an opaque store id and there is **no date**, so an entry recalled from days ago is textually indistinguishable from the live user message it is prepended to.
  - Renders the entry's storage date, which `MemoryEntry.timestamp` already carries and the renderer ignored: `- [from 2026-09-01] {key}: {content}`. (`[from]`, not `[recalled]`: the timestamp is when the entry was stored, and the recall happens now — labelling it the recall date would itself be the class of ambiguity this PR removes.)
  - Gated by a new `memory.recall_date_stamp` key, **default on**. An entry the model mistakes for live input is wrong on every deployment and the change is additive text on a line that already exists — but a deployment that needs byte-stable injection output can switch it off.
  - `stored_on` takes the `YYYY-MM-DD` prefix only when the value is shaped like an RFC3339 date, so a backend storing anything else keeps the untagged line rather than surfacing a half-parsed one. Prefix check, not a parse: no new dependency, and it cannot panic on a multi-byte timestamp.

### The failure this fixes

On a tool-using agent that writes structured records, a numeric value from a message recalled from **two days earlier** was copied into a tool call made for the live message, which supplied no such value. The record written was wrong in a way nothing downstream could detect, because the value was well-formed and plausible.

The model's own reasoning named the memory block as its source. In other turns on the same agent it described that block as "confusing", "weird", and "probably other users" — it can tell something is off in the input and has no field that would let it say what. Fourteen turns in one session cited the block; three complained about it.

This is not a retrieval-quality problem. The right entries were recalled. They were rendered without the one attribute that makes them safe to read.

### Trade-offs

- **The stamp is charged to `max_total_chars`**, like the rest of the line — about 17 characters per entry. A tight character budget therefore fits one fewer entry. That is deliberate: an unlabelled entry the model mistakes for live input is worse than one entry fewer, and the tight-budget golden pins the cost so it cannot regress silently. The entry-count cap is unaffected; the two cases now have separate goldens.
- **Golden tests gained a clock dependency** once dates entered the output, and the corpus deliberately holds one entry aged 60 days, so expectations need two different dates. `golden_corpus` now takes the clock as a parameter and the goldens are templated on `{today}` / `{stale}`, so an expectation cannot straddle a UTC midnight mid-test.

- **Scope boundary:** Does not change what is recalled, ranked, filtered, decayed, or budgeted — only how a surviving entry is rendered. Does not touch the `[Memory context]` wrapper, the skip set, the rerank stage, or `MemoryEntry`.
- **Blast radius:** With the gate on (default), every agent that injects memory sees ~17 more characters per rendered entry, and a deployment sitting exactly on `max_total_chars` renders one fewer entry; `recall_date_stamp = false` restores the previous output byte-for-byte. Contains-style assertions that pinned the old `- {key}:` line prefix now anchor on `{key}: {content}` alone, so they keep proving the pipeline behaviour they were written for without pinning the line shape; the goldens pin the exact shape.
- **Linked issue(s):** None
- **Labels:** `type:feat`, `memory`

## Testing (required)

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes — the render change is visible in one turn with any memory backend that returns a hit.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface: cli` and `channel` — injection is shared by both.
- **Setup / preconditions:** any agent with a memory backend that recalls at least one entry (`[agent.memory]`, backend `sqlite`).
- **Steps to run:** store a memory, then send a turn whose text recalls it, with `RUST_LOG=zeroclaw_runtime::agent=debug`.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** the injected block reads `- [from YYYY-MM-DD] {key}: {content}`.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** the same line without the date — identical in shape to the live user turn beneath it.
- **Gate off (`recall_date_stamp = false`):** identical to `master`.

prs.title: feat(zerocode): show saved and applied config status
prs.body:
> [!NOTE]
> This PR is stacked on #11466 at `feb7f313406c78fdd731d8ceaf13f20cd95ed94a`, which depends on #10911. Review the [owned child change](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/compare/feb7f313406c78fdd731d8ceaf13f20cd95ed94a...84835a1a527c53b03ab086f5550fbd4b3cf44be4).

## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. GitHub shows the cumulative stack; the owned comparison above isolates this change.
- **What changed and why:** Return the exact committed revision from Config set/delete and changed map-key operations. Use it to distinguish a successful save from each running target's acknowledged application.
- **Scope boundary:** Consume the existing application ledger and authenticated status RPC. Keep reload explicit. No new application consumers, ledger, watcher, or persistence mechanism.
- **Blast radius:** ZeroCode Config rendering, status polling, and additive mutation-result fields. Existing callers can ignore the optional receipt.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11491. Depends on #11466 and #10911. Related #10892 and #11436.
- **Runtime placement:** Depends on #11436. The covering scope needs a recorded Core Team decision in the exception table before this implementation merges.
- **Labels:** `enhancement`, `docs`, `dependencies`, `core`, `agent`, `channel`, `config`, `cron`, `daemon`, `gateway`, `provider`, `runtime`, `skills`, `tool`, `tests`, `channel:core`, `channel:telegram`, `channel:matrix`, `tool:delegate`, `channel:whatsapp`, `security:pairing`, `stacked`, `quickstart`, `zerocode`, `risk:high`, `channel:line`, `size:XL`, `channel:acp`, `channel:wechat`, `cli`. The cumulative stack includes the parent's runtime changes; the owned child is an ordinary behavioral change.

### What this does, simply

ZeroCode Config lets an operator save settings for a running ZeroClaw. A successful save tells them the value was persisted, but it does not tell them whether a running session accepted it or whether the daemon still needs a reload.

This PR keeps that save result visible and shows the backend's separate outcomes: Applied live, Pending, Rejected, Reload required, or Application status unavailable. Press `s` outside an editor or search field to open the details, including the changed path, saved revision, and target instance. A session can have applied a change while the daemon still requires reload.

Each save receives its own revision from the commit that persisted it. A later writer's change cannot acknowledge that save. Missing records, a replacement daemon, unsupported status, unknown outcomes, and failed reads remain unavailable. Reading status never reloads the daemon.

### Scope and maintenance tradeoff

The owned child changes 11 files with approximately 600 production lines; much of the remaining delta is targeted tests. GitHub's cumulative comparison includes 67 files from the dependency stack. The existing backend owns publication, authorization, application acknowledgement, and bounded retention. The new client module owns only decoding, one background poll, revision filtering, and the summary/detail view.

Returning the commit's revision is required to avoid attributing a later status read to the wrong save. Per-target details are required because one global Applied banner cannot represent a live session and a daemon awaiting reload. Batch RPC writes and alias rename are outside this client's exercised write paths. Local ZeroCode settings, personality files, and skill files retain their separate save feedback.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, for actual terminal presentation.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface: tui`, ZeroCode Config.
- **Setup / preconditions:** Run ZeroCode and the daemon from this stack, using an existing authorized profile and agent. The daemon must support the parent's application-status contract.
- **Steps to run:** Open Config. Change one existing non-secret scalar setting and save it. Wait for status, then press `s` outside an editor. Scroll with Up/Down and Page Up/Page Down. Escape returns to Config. Restore the original value afterward; use the existing explicit reload action only if needed.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The summary distinguishes Saved from application outcomes. Details identify canonical path components, exact revision, and daemon/session target. The summary and help remain readable at 120 columns by 40 rows and 80 columns by 24 rows; details can scroll without editing the hidden Config field.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** Config provides save/reload feedback but no per-target application summary or revision detail view.

### How I tested

At `3dbb5f06c9545bcf4325f64b1080563539931326` (before the restack onto the parent's current head; not rerun since, because the parent itself no longer builds against master):

```text
cargo fmt --all -- --check
Passed.

cargo nextest run --locked -p zerocode -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib --bin zerocode --build-jobs 4 -j 2 -E 'test(config_application) | test(config_manager::tests::) | test(keymap::) | test(config_set_save_failure_leaves_published_pair_unchanged) | test(config_delete_provider_temperature_refreshes_matching_live_session)'
144 tests run: 144 passed, 6794 skipped.

bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh
Passed.

DOCS_FILES=docs/book/src/zerocode/config.md bash scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh
Summary: 0 error(s).
```

The focused tests exercise real RPC dispatch for committed receipts, failed persistence, no-op map operations, and a session acknowledgement. Client tests exercise later writers, replaced epochs, unavailable/unknown status, pending settlement, and stale poll cancellation. A Config save-hook test drives the actual Config renderer through `ratatui::TestBackend`; this is supplementary automated evidence, not a terminal screenshot. Matching default-feature ZeroCode and daemon binaries also built with `cargo build --locked -p zerocode -p zeroclaw --bin zerocode --bin zeroclaw -j 4`. The macOS debug linker warned about a large unwind section in the test harness and daemon binary; compilation and all selected tests succeeded.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** [Quality Gate](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/37143077875) passed on this exact head, covering cumulative workspace lint, tests, feature/target compilation, formatting, docs, and applicable Windows/runtime checks.
- **Known CI coverage gap:** Real terminal clipping, wrapping, and visible scroll affordances require direct capture.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** I used it in the experiment build: saved a daemon setting, read the one-line summary, opened the change log with `s`, and checked a fresh daemon with no changes. The wording in this PR comes from that.
- **Visual interface evidence:** I'm verifying this in the [experiment build](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/tree/experiment/zerocode-builds/20261014T024640Z-eb55856696a7). My screenshots from that build are in [this comment](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11506#issuecomment-6160142675).
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Broad local workspace checks are left to current-head CI; the focused tests cover the owned behavior.

### Visual evidence

I'm verifying this in the experiment build [`20261014T024640Z-eb55856696a7`](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/tree/experiment/zerocode-builds/20261014T024640Z-eb55856696a7) ([commit](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/commit/eb55856696a7a54506c14f54b0ffe0eca9816a7e); dogfood base [`dogfood/zerocode-builds/20261008T194402Z-0341618f9d69`](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/tree/dogfood/zerocode-builds/20261008T194402Z-0341618f9d69)); screenshots in [this comment](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11506#issuecomment-6160142675). What a save shows now:

- One yellow line, for example: `Saved "hooks.enabled". Please reload the daemon (⌘R) to apply this change. Press s to view the log.` Other outcomes: already applied, applying, rejected by a session, open sessions only, or can't confirm.
- `s` opens the **Config change log**. The hint is left off while it's open. The `s` binding and hint appear only after a save or when the daemon has recent changes.
- A fresh daemon with no changes shows "No config changes since the daemon started."

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No.
- New external network calls? No. Status uses the existing configured daemon RPC connection.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No.

Status stays behind the existing authenticated RPC authorization. The view displays canonical paths, revision identifiers, target context, and fixed outcome/reason labels, not configuration values or raw provider errors. Unknown wire values are conservative.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes. Mutation receipts are additive optional fields; absent receipts or status display unavailable.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes. ZeroCode adds the configurable `application_status` shortcut and detail-navigation actions. No daemon config migration is required.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No.
- Upgrade steps: Use matching ZeroCode and daemon versions for the new feedback. Existing keybinding configuration remains valid; `s` is the default outside text entry.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** Revert the owned child commits in reverse order, `git revert 84835a1a527c 29c07fb97294 c260fc2e4c8d 9f5451079e52 e8e6043e3568 013d700865db d0bef2381131`, or deploy the previous matching ZeroCode/daemon build. The parent remains a separate dependency.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None. The detail view is opened explicitly; reload retains its existing confirmation.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** Application status remains unavailable after an acknowledged edit, shows the wrong revision/target, or the summary/help clips in a narrow terminal. Save and reload errors retain their existing reporting.

prs.title: test(ci): require real application acceptance
prs.body:
## Summary

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Base branch:** | `master` |
| **Scope boundary:** | Linux, default features, and fake external HTTP services. Browser UI, other operating systems, real vendor availability/model quality, and release-package installation are future coverage. |
| **Blast radius:** | Required CI selection/build duration and daemon remote-TUI identity initialization. No new production config, public API, dependency, or security bypass. |
| **Linked issue(s):** | Motivated by the reported local ZeroCode startup regression after OIDC work. The exact historical revision is unknown; the synthetic saved-config test does not claim to reproduce it. |
| **Labels:** | `ci`, `docs`, `daemon`, `runtime`, `tests`, `scripts`, `risk:high`, `size:XL`, `type:ci`. |

### What changed and why:

- Build the actual ZeroClaw and ZeroCode binaries together in the existing Linux build, then exercise user workflows before that required dependency succeeds.
- Add isolated core/full acceptance suites, a conservative path/label selector, and controlled faults that prove the harness detects failures.
- Reevaluate on PR updates and changes to `risk:high`, `domain:security`, `priority:p0`, or `priority:p1`; run full for merge queue, master pushes, and ordinary manual dispatch. Unrelated label events allocate no runners or replace required-check evidence. Skip added ZeroCode compilation when acceptance is skipped, and reject an unexpectedly skipped build in `CI Required Gate`.
- Fix a production defect found by the WSS scenario: the daemon loaded the TUI signing key from `data/.secret_key`, although the normal config CLI writes it at the installation root. Resolve the existing key through `Config::install_root_dir()`.

### What this does, simply

A successful compile does not prove that the applications work together. This check starts the daemon, drives the real ZeroCode terminal, and requires a completed conversation, approved/denied file writes, a completed SOP, records that survive restart, and working authentication.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
PR[PR merge commit] --> Build[Build both applications once]
Build --> Select[Core or full acceptance]
Select --> Evidence[Results and sanitized evidence]
Select --> Gate[CI Required Gate]
```

Each test creates temporary config, storage, sockets, ports, signing keys, and external API fixtures. There is no model installation, vendor API key, or manual setup beyond normal build prerequisites, Python 3.9+, tmux, and OpenSSL. CI installs the prerequisites.

The core budget is five minutes and the full budget is ten minutes, excluding compilation; the Linux job has a 60-minute timeout. Read-only PR permissions, pinned actions, and master-only cache writes remain in effect.

> The WSS test failed against the original daemon with `Remote RPC requires signed TUI identities (-32010)`, despite provisioning a credential through the normal CLI and issuing a client certificate. With the canonical key-path fix, both native and OIDC WSS conversations complete with server-certificate verification enabled.

---

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Reviewer testing requested?** | Yes, the shared command exercises the complete application boundary. |
| **Interface(s) exercised:** | `surface=cli`, `surface=tui`, and `surface=web` for HTTP API calls; local Unix RPC and remote WSS. |
| **Setup / preconditions:** | Linux, normal Rust/system build dependencies, Python 3.9+, tmux, OpenSSL. No credentials or installed model required. |

#### Steps to run:

```sh
scripts/ci/runtime_acceptance.sh --suite core --artifacts-dir /tmp/acceptance-core
scripts/ci/runtime_acceptance.sh --suite full --artifacts-dir /tmp/acceptance-full
# Reuse binaries to avoid another build:
scripts/ci/runtime_acceptance.sh --suite full --bin-dir target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/ci --artifacts-dir /tmp/acceptance-full-reuse
python3 tests/system/runtime_acceptance/test_faults.py --bin-dir target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/ci --artifacts-dir /tmp/acceptance-faults
```

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Expected on this branch (after):** | All selected scenarios execute and pass; negative controls each return a nonzero scenario result and the fault-check command succeeds. Inspect JSON/JUnit, terminal captures, fixture counts, and sanitized logs. |
| **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** | There is no required executable acceptance suite. Running the new harness against unpatched binaries reproduces the WSS signing-key failure above. No claim is made about the unidentified historical OIDC startup revision. |

### How I tested

#### CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:

Local application and workflow checks below passed. [Final PR Quality Gate run 36837037785](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36837037785) tests head `e7b34e4b6b` through merge commit `016f34e26eb129f17fcaf9c01bef154ea1b30366`. Full acceptance passed in **66.735 seconds**, and all three negative controls passed their failure-detection assertions. **All Quality Gate jobs passed, including `CI Required Gate`.** Its Linux build owns acceptance failures. The earlier implementation also passed [run 36803070859](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36803070859).

> **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** Linux/default-feature acceptance only. The external services are scripted fixtures; they do not measure vendor availability or model quality.

<details>
<summary>Commands run and tail output:</summary>

Initial implementation validation on Linux aarch64 in Docker, Rust 1.98.0, default features, locked dependencies:

```text
cargo build --locked --profile ci -p zeroclaw -p zerocode --bins
Finished ci profile: initial build 5m11s; rebuild with the daemon fix 5m26s

scripts/ci/runtime_acceptance.sh --suite core --bin-dir target/ci --artifacts-dir /tmp/acceptance-core-final
5 scenario groups passed; 38.218 seconds

scripts/ci/runtime_acceptance.sh --suite full --bin-dir target/ci --artifacts-dir /tmp/acceptance-full-final

python3 tests/system/runtime_acceptance/test_faults.py --bin-dir target/ci --artifacts-dir /tmp/acceptance-faults-final

Negative control response: detected (13.381s)
Negative control sop: detected (9.088s)

python3 tests/system/runtime_acceptance/test_contracts.py

cargo test --locked --profile ci --test architecture ci_runner_labels

cargo fmt --all -- --check
bash -n scripts/ci/runtime_acceptance.sh

Summary: 0 error(s)

Ran 6 tests ... OK; no added links
```

</details>

Additional validation for the cost changes: **15 Python selector/fixture/workflow contracts passed**, including execution of the actual workflow build script with captured Cargo arguments and a forced Cargo failure. `actionlint`, formatting, and documentation gates passed. The rebuilt architecture harness passed the nine runner checks; its full set of **55 architecture tests** then passed against the updated workflow after preserving the existing debounce and release-preflight conditions.

### CI cost and trigger policy

The [controlled Blacksmith measurement](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36835567811) used one **8-vCPU Linux x86_64 runner**, Rust 1.98.0, default features, locked dependencies, and the same target path. Before each build it restored the identical initial target snapshot; dependencies were fetched before timing. The cache reported an exact hit. Build order was baseline/candidate/candidate/baseline.

| Measurement | Existing build | Build with acceptance |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| First build sample | 176.706s | 173.249s |
| Second build sample | 157.832s | 171.779s |
| Mean compilation time | **167.269s** | **172.514s** |
| Added mean compilation | | **5.245s** |
| Core execution | | **36.798s** |
| Full execution | | **65.599s** |
| Full failure-detection controls | | **23.644s** |

The compilation difference is small relative to the variation between samples; **5.245s is a measured mean, not a guaranteed overhead**. The benchmark ran at `6891a0817c`. Subsequent commits only preserved existing CI predicates and their tests; the measured application source, Cargo commands, runner/cache setup, and acceptance scenarios are unchanged. Both suites and all three negative controls passed. Results, binary hashes, and logs are in the seven-day `acceptance-cost` artifact. The one-off measurement job consumed **14m18s**, about **$0.23** at the public compute rate before allowances.

| Event | Work performed | Required-check behavior |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Ordinary code update | Existing quality workflow plus selected core/full acceptance | `CI Required Gate` requires a successful build |
| Documentation-only update without a full-suite label | Existing quality checks; acceptance and added ZeroCode build skipped | Existing quality gate still runs |
| Unrelated label change | **No runners allocated** | Separate concurrency group; no check named `CI Required Gate` |
| Risk/security/urgent-priority label change | Full quality workflow reruns and reevaluates the suite | Preserves the original plan's merge-blocking behavior |
| Explicit `acceptance_cost=true` manual dispatch | Only the bounded measurement job | Cannot satisfy or replace `CI Required Gate`; never writes shared caches |

Live unrelated-label tests [36835638327](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36835638327) and [36835640659](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36835640659) each had **36 skipped jobs, zero assigned runners, and no `CI Required Gate` check**. The active quality run continued. These ran before the two preserved legacy predicates were restored; those predicates already exclude label events through a push-only condition or the guarded detector dependency.

In the final PR run, the Linux build job (including acceptance and its existing voice-wake test) took **7.18 minutes**. It finished before **Test Windows task-owner recovery**, the last quality dependency. Acceptance was therefore not the pacing job in that observed run; other PRs and cache states can differ.

#### Added compute at the public rate

[Blacksmith's public pricing](https://www.blacksmith.sh/pricing), checked on October 1, 2026, shows **$0.016/minute for 8-vCPU Ubuntu x64** and **$0.008/minute for 4-vCPU Ubuntu x64**. These calculations exclude allowances, sponsorship, billing rounding, storage, and setup/artifact overhead that the paired Cargo measurement does not isolate.

| Selected suite | Added build + execution | Added 8-vCPU runner-minutes | Compute at public rate |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Core | 42.043s | 0.701 | **$0.0112/run** |
| Full, including failure controls | 94.488s | 1.575 | **$0.0252/run** |

The seven complete UTC days **September 24–30** contained **1,198 Quality Gate runs**: 889 PR, 123 push, and 186 merge-queue runs. Counts include failed and cancelled runs. Extrapolating that request volume to 30 days gives these reference scenarios; they are **not invoice forecasts** and assume every counted run reaches acceptance. Documentation-only skips and cancellations can reduce usage.

| 30-day acceptance scenario | Added 8-vCPU runner-minutes | Compute before allowances |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Every PR uses core; pushes and merge queue use full | **4,755** | **$76** |
| Every run uses full | **8,085** | **$129** |

#### Risk-label workflow reruns are a separate cost

Relevant label changes still rerun the whole quality workflow in this version. Three recent successful PR baselines consumed **53.318, 94.867, and 95.766 Blacksmith runner-minutes** across the 4-/8-vCPU classes, or **$0.82–$1.47 per complete workflow** at public rates before acceptance is added. Their total runner usage including GitHub-hosted platforms was 73.651, 136.534, and 115.566 minutes: [run 36791618917](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36791618917), [run 36785496319](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36785496319), [run 36776032033](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36776032033). These are observational workflow samples, not a controlled comparison of identical changes.

The same week recorded **138 relevant label events across 81 PRs** (133 additions, five removals). If every event caused an additional complete workflow at the sampled costs, a 30-day extrapolation would add roughly **$502–$882**, including full acceptance, **on top of** the acceptance-only figures above. Eligibility, concurrency cancellation, and overlapping events can reduce that scenario; it is not a claim about actual invoices or future event volume. Unrelated-label reruns now cost zero runner time.

The public OSS program does not establish this project's agreement. **The project's actual Blacksmith allowance, sponsorship, and effective rates remain unconfirmed**: the available dashboard session is signed out. The owner must confirm those terms before interpreting the public-rate scenarios as a budget.

<details>
<summary>Reproduce the measurement and usage calculation</summary>

```sh
gh workflow run ci.yml --ref <branch> -f acceptance_cost=true
gh run download <run-id> --name acceptance-cost
```

`measurement.json` records each Cargo command, sample duration, cache status, platform, revision, and suite durations. Added per-run minutes are `(candidate_mean - baseline_mean + suite_seconds + applicable_fault_seconds) / 60`. Thirty-day scenarios multiply observed weekly event counts by `30 / 7` and the per-run minutes.

Workflow counts came from the `actions/workflows/ci.yml/runs` API, paginated separately for each UTC date to avoid the 1,000-result search limit. Runner-minutes sum `completed_at - started_at` for assigned jobs from each run's `/jobs` API and group them by runner label. Risk-label counts came from 58 pages of repository issue events covering the same window, filtering PR label additions/removals to the canonical four labels. These counts describe requests and events, not billed minutes.

</details>

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** | Inspected real rendered terminal output, approval results and filesystem effects, the pre-fix WSS failure, post-fix native/OIDC conversations, and sanitized artifacts. These scenarios are automated keyboard/API interactions; no separate manual UI run is claimed. |
| **Visual interface evidence:** | N/A for layout changes. Existing terminal output is asserted through tmux at 120×45 cells, English locale, and terminal lifecycle titles. No visual presentation code changes. |
| **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** | Final implementation head `e7b34e4b6b`; the final PR acceptance run records merge SHA `016f34e26eb129f17fcaf9c01bef154ea1b30366` and its binary hashes. The paired cost measurement records `6891a0817c` and its binary hashes separately. Initial local evidence remains recorded in `results.json` (the full suite repeated after the unexpected-exit assertion took 67.062s). Artifact `runtime-acceptance` contains `selection.json`, `scenarios/results.json`, `scenarios/junit.xml`, per-scenario captures/logs, and negative-control diagnostics; retention is seven days. |
| **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** | Terminal assertions include `REPLY_WARM`, `REPLY_NATIVE_REMOTE`, `REPLY_OIDC_REMOTE`, `TOOL_APPROVED`, and `TOOL_DENIED`, followed by the idle title `✓ acceptance`. SOP writes `SOP_COMPLETE`; its completed record and `PERSISTED_MEMORY` are retrieved after restart. |
| **Action or changed state and observed result:** | Enter approves a file write; Ctrl+D denies another without creating a file. RPC/HTTP permission revocation is observed across the opposite interface and requires OIDC reauthentication. Invalid tokens cannot enter RPC or the HTTP agent endpoint. Missing response or SOP progress fails with a bounded diagnostic. |
| **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** | Full local Clippy/workspace/platform validation is delegated to normal PR CI. No additional model or external vendor test was run. The existing PR CI lint, workspace, architecture, platform, and Windows recovery checks subsequently all passed. |

---

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? | **No** for production. The runner operates only its temporary installations and identifies owned processes before cleanup. |
| New external network calls? | **No** for production; test services bind loopback. CI uses its existing dependency/action infrastructure. |
| Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? | **Yes.** The daemon reads the existing TUI signing key from the same installation-root location used by config persistence. This restores signed remote identities without weakening bearer authentication or mTLS. Test credentials/keys are generated or synthetic; uploaded evidence is sanitized and excludes configs, databases, tokens, and private-key files. |
| PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? | **No.** |
| Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? | **No** for production; fixtures supply fixed test prompts/responses. |

**If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation:** The remote-identity initialization change is verified by real certificate issuance, verified WSS connections, and production native/OIDC verification. Existing permission checks remain active.

## Compatibility (required)

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Backward compatible? | **Yes.** |
| Config / env / CLI surface changed? | **No** for the applications. The new local test command accepts `--suite`, `--bin-dir`, and `--artifacts-dir`. Quality Gate adds an opt-in `acceptance_cost` manual-dispatch input; its default remains the full quality workflow. |
| Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? | **No.** |
| Exact upgrade steps: | None. |

---

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Fast rollback command/path:** | Revert the acceptance integration in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and its harness if it causes CI failures unrelated to application regressions. A complete rollback is `git revert <merge-commit>`. Retain the general required `CI Required Gate` rule; the signing-key path correction can be retained independently. |
| **Feature flags or config toggles:** | No runtime feature flags. Routine path/label selection controls core/full; it is not a failure bypass. The opt-in `acceptance_cost` workflow input selects a separate measurement run and cannot satisfy the required quality check. |
| **Observable failure symptoms:** | Failed Linux build/`CI Required Gate`; scenario name, error, timings and unexecuted selected scenarios in JSON/JUnit; sanitized daemon and terminal artifacts identify initialization, response, auth, or SOP failures. |

### Merge enforcement rollout

**Incomplete: repository administrator action is required.** After the PR acceptance suite passed, the authorized `PUT /repos/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/rulesets/23991526` returned HTTP 404. The same account can read the ruleset and push PRs, but its repository permissions report `admin: false`. Readback confirmed the active [master ruleset](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/rules/23991526) is unchanged and still contains only its merge queue rule.

An administrator must add the required status check **`CI Required Gate`**, sourced from **GitHub Actions** (integration ID `15368`), to that existing ruleset, preserving the merge queue, branch conditions, bypass actors, and all unrelated rules. Keep strict up-to-date checks disabled because the merge queue validates the combined commit. Read back the master branch rules to verify enforcement. The workflow implementation is complete, but automatic merge blocking is not fully rolled out until this setting is applied.

prs.title: fix(zerocode): make Shift+Tab match its default bindings
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Shift+Tab did nothing in zerocode on real terminals. Terminals report it as `BackTab` with Shift set (crossterm 0.29 does this for the legacy `CSI Z` sequence in `event/sys/unix/parse.rs`, for the enhanced keyboard protocol, and on Windows), while the default bindings are `BackTab` with no modifiers and `Chord::matches` compares modifiers exactly.
  - Three default bindings never fired: Config's previous sub-tab (`config_tab.section_prev`), Dashboard's previous tab (`dashboard.prev_tab`), and the quickstart modals' previous field (`quickstart_modal.prev_field`). The Config and Dashboard help overlays list Shift+Tab.
  - `strip_redundant_shift` now treats the Shift as implied by `BackTab`, the way it already does for shifted glyphs, so bindings and events compare the same way. A Shift+Tab captured in the binding editor (which records the event verbatim) also renders once as `Shift+Tab` instead of `Shift+Shift+Tab`.
- **Scope boundary:** Matching and display of `BackTab` only. No binding, action, or override format changes; a `shift+tab` written by hand in a keybinding override still parses as Tab with Shift, which terminals never send.
- **Blast radius:** zerocode key dispatch for `BackTab`. Ctrl+Shift+Tab and other combinations keep their own modifiers, so they still do not match a bare `BackTab` binding.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11263 (its Config docs avoid promising Shift+Tab because of this bug).
- **Labels:** (maintainer-applied)

### What this does, simply

Shift+Tab is meant to go back one sub-tab in Config, one tab on the Dashboard, and one field in the quickstart forms, and the Config and Dashboard help say so, but pressing it did nothing. The terminal sends Shift+Tab with the Shift key marked as held, and zerocode only accepted it without that mark. This makes zerocode accept the key the way terminals actually send it.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface=tui`
- **Setup / preconditions:** Any running daemon of the same version.
- **Steps to run:** Open zerocode, go to the Config tab, press Shift+Tab. Repeat on the Dashboard tabs and inside a quickstart modal form.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** Config moves to the previous sub-tab (wrapping from `zeroclaw` to `zerocode`), the Dashboard moves to the previous tab, and the quickstart form moves to the previous field.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** Shift+Tab does nothing in all three places.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Required CI covers the zerocode crate this change is limited to.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** CI does not drive a real terminal; the pty run below covers that.
- **Commands run and tail output:** (head `5a6fbb2fda`, on master `83f0ff3805`)

```text
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
(no output)
$ cargo clippy -p zerocode --all-targets -- -D warnings
Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s)
$ cargo test -p zerocode
test result: ok. 1401 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
$ bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh apps/zerocode/src/keymap/chord.rs apps/zerocode/src/keymap/mod.rs
Comment hygiene gate passed.
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Ran the real zerocode binary in an 80x24 pty against a running daemon and sent the byte sequence a terminal sends for Shift+Tab (`ESC [ Z`) in the Config tab. Before (master binary): the `zeroclaw` sub-tab stayed selected. After (this branch): the first press selected `zerocode`, the second returned to `zeroclaw`. The new tests were mutation-checked: removing the `BackTab` clause fails all three. Not verified by hand: the Dashboard and quickstart bindings beyond the keymap test, and Windows terminals (crossterm's Windows parser produces the same `BackTab` plus Shift event).
- **Visual interface evidence:** Screenshot
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `5a6fbb2fda` and master, zerocode in an 80x24 pty; the raw terminal output was replayed in xterm.js to produce the images.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** before and after screenshots are attached in a PR comment.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** `ESC [ Z` in the Config tab: before, no change; after, the selected sub-tab moves from `zeroclaw` to `zerocode`, and back on a second press.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** `cargo check --workspace` was not run locally because only zerocode changed; CI runs it.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? `No`
- New external network calls? `No`
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? `No`
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? `No`
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? `No`
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? `Yes`
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? `No`
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? `No`
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: N/A

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Low risk: `git revert <merged-squash-sha>`.

prs.title: test(hardware): pass arduino-cli flags through the Windows fake
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - The advisory Windows job always runs `cargo nextest run -p zeroclaw-hardware --features hardware --lib`, whatever a PR touches. Two `arduino_upload` tests fail there, so every `ci:windows` run has been red since at least 2026-09-26, whatever the PR under test changed.
  - `fake_cli_success_runs_all_stages_and_cleans_workspace`: the Windows fake `arduino-cli` is a PowerShell script whose `param()` block uses `[Parameter(ValueFromRemainingArguments = $true)]`. That attribute makes it an advanced script. Windows PowerShell then reads the upload stage's `-p` as the abbreviated `-PipelineVariable` common parameter and swallows the port value with it, so the logged call never starts with `upload -p`. The fake now reads its arguments from `$args` in a plain script, where `-p` passes through unchanged. The product command line (`upload -p <port> --fqbn <fqbn> <sketch>`) is unchanged and correct.
  - `failed_preflight_does_not_compile_or_upload`: PowerShell's `Add-Content` ends each logged line with CRLF on Windows, and the test compared the log with `"version\n"` byte for byte. It now compares the logged calls line by line, like the neighboring assertions.
- **Scope boundary:** Test-only. No change to `ArduinoUploadTool`, its arguments, timeouts, process handling, or the Unix fake.
- **Blast radius:** Two tests in `crates/zeroclaw-hardware/src/peripherals/arduino_upload.rs`.
- **Linked issue(s):** None filed; no issue tracks the advisory Windows failures. Related: the sibling PRs listed at the end.
- **Labels:** `ci:windows` (opts this PR into the advisory Windows job). Path, size, and `risk:*` labels come from the labelers and maintainers.

### What this does, simply

The Arduino upload tool is tested against a fake `arduino-cli` that records how it was called. On Windows the fake is a PowerShell script, and PowerShell quietly took the tool's `-p` (port) flag for one of its own options, so the record never showed the upload call the test looks for. The record also ended lines with Windows line endings, which one test did not expect. The fake now passes every flag through untouched, and the test compares lines rather than raw bytes. Nothing about the real tool changes; this only stops two tests from failing on every Windows run.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, on Windows only; the Unix fake is a shell script and was never affected.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** None user-facing; hardware tool unit tests with a fake CLI.
- **Setup / preconditions:** A Windows machine with the MSVC toolchain and Windows PowerShell, or the `ci:windows` label on this PR.
- **Steps to run:** `cargo nextest run -p zeroclaw-hardware --features hardware --lib arduino_upload::`
- **Expected on this branch (after):** All `arduino_upload` tests pass.

prs.title: fix(providers): custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints default to native tool calling
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - **Default flip.** `CustomModelProviderConfig::create_provider` disabled native tool calling unless `native_tools` was explicitly `Some(true)`, so custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints (vLLM, llama.cpp, LiteLLM and similar, which mostly support native function calling) used prompt-guided XML tools by default. It now disables them only for `native_tools == Some(false)`.
  - **Runtime fallback for endpoints that reject native tools.** If a `custom.<alias>` provider answers a native-tools request with a 400/422 that names `tools`, `tool_choice` or function calling (`rejects_native_tool_calling`), the turn retries once with prompt-guided tools: the prompt anchor and scoped tool-protocol prompt switch to the text protocol, the tool instructions are added when missing, and a warning names the alias and the exact line (`[providers.models.custom.<alias>] native_tools = false`) that skips the failing request next time. The downgrade is remembered for the rest of the turn (keyed by provider), so later iterations do not resend the rejected request. The provider-internal schema fallback in `compatible.rs` is skipped for the Custom family so this one path owns the decision and the warning, and the streaming path in `provider_call.rs` hands a native-tools rejection back to the runtime instead of re-sending non-streaming.
  - **`stream_chat` dedup.** `OpenAiResponsesModelProvider::stream_chat` now reuses the already-tested `build_request()` (adds `#[derive(Clone)]`); no behavior change.
- **Scope boundary:** the `custom` family default, the fallback above, and the Responses streaming dedup. Other families keep their defaults (Groq still defaults to text fallback).
- **Blast radius:** operators of custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints that never set `native_tools` now get native tool calling; an endpoint that rejects it is downgraded per turn with a warning. `zeroclaw-providers` (factory, `compatible.rs`, `openai.rs`), `zeroclaw-config` (doc comment only) and the runtime turn loop.
- **Linked issue(s):** None
- **Labels:** `bug`, `docs`, `agent`, `config`, `provider`, `runtime`, `distinguished contributor`, `provider:openai`, `provider:compatible`, `needs-author-action`, `risk:medium`, `size:L`, `topic:provider-transport`

Rebased on current master (`f504602a9`). Conflicts were in `turn/mod.rs` (upstream replaced `try_reserve_shared_iteration` with the execution-tree budget) and `turn/provider_call.rs` (terminal stream errors are now returned directly instead of re-running non-streaming chat). Both intents are kept; the native-tools rejection check runs before the terminal/non-terminal stream handling.

### What this does, simply

When you point ZeroClaw at your own OpenAI-compatible server, it used to talk to it with text-based tool instructions unless you had explicitly turned native tool calling on, even if the server handles native function calls. Now native tool calling is the default for those servers. If a server cannot do it and says so, ZeroClaw switches that turn to text-based tools, tells you which alias it happened for and how to make the switch permanent (`native_tools = false`), and keeps using text tools for the rest of that turn instead of failing or asking again.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Optional.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** any surface (`cli`, `tui`, `channel`) running a turn through a `custom` provider alias.
- **Setup / preconditions:** a `[providers.models.custom.<alias>]` entry pointing at an endpoint that returns HTTP 400 for requests containing `tools` (a small local mock is enough).
- **Steps to run:** run a turn that needs a tool through that alias.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** one native attempt is rejected, the turn completes over prompt-guided tools, one warning names the alias and `native_tools = false`, and later iterations of the same turn send no native request.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** the alias used prompt-guided tools from the start unless `native_tools = true` was set; there is no fallback if native tools are enabled and rejected.

### How I tested

Run on an arm64 Linux host with the CI toolchain (1.98.0) at the pushed head.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the required `Lint`, `Check`, `Test` and `Parallel Runtime Test` jobs cover `zeroclaw-providers`, `zeroclaw-config` and `zeroclaw-runtime`, the crates touched.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** none known.
- **Commands run and tail output:**
  ```
  cargo fmt --all -- --check                                            clean
  scripts/ci/run_clippy.sh --scope workspace (all targets, -D warnings)   clean
  cargo check --locked --features ci-all --all-targets                  clean
  cargo check --locked --no-default-features                            clean
  cargo test --locked --test architecture                               55 passed
  cargo nextest run --locked -p zeroclaw-providers                      1979 tests run: 1979 passed, 7 skipped
  cargo nextest run --locked -p zeroclaw-config                         1874 tests run: 1874 passed
  cargo nextest run --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime                        5334 tests run: 5334 passed, 8 skipped
  cargo doc --no-deps --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop            ok
  scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh                                    passed
  ```
  New or updated tests: `custom_factory_enables_native_tools_by_default` and `custom_factory_honors_native_tools_override_false` (factory default and opt-out); `native_tool_rejection_detection_matches_400_tools_errors` and `native_tool_rejection_detection_ignores_unrelated_provider_errors` (matcher, with 401, unknown-model and reasoning-effort negatives); `custom_native_tools_rejection_falls_back_to_prompt_guided_tools_with_alias_warning` (local endpoint rejects native tools, the turn completes over two iterations, exactly one native request is sent, the prompt-guided request carries the tool instructions, the warning names the alias and `native_tools = false`; with the per-turn downgrade disabled it fails with 2 native requests); `prompt_guided_instructions_are_inserted_when_no_system_message_exists`; and `turn_rebuilds_prompt_for_vision_routed_xml_provider`, which now models the no-native-tools vision provider through an explicit alias with `native_tools = false`.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** The rebase conflict resolution by reading both sides against upstream's new stream handling. Not verified: a real vLLM/llama.cpp endpoint, and an SSE-shaped mid-stream native-tools rejection (the streaming hand-off in `provider_call.rs` is reviewed but only the non-streaming rejection is exercised end to end).
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A (no rendered interface state changed; the warning is a status line and log event).
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** the pushed head of this PR; no interface capture.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** see the fallback test above.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** none skipped.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No (at most one extra request to the already configured endpoint after a rejection)
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No (the rejection text passes through `scrub_credentials` before it is logged)
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No (the fallback reuses the existing text tool-instruction builder)
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? No, mildly: custom endpoints that support native tools now use them by default, and endpoints that reject them are downgraded per turn with a warning instead of using text tools from the first request.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No new keys; the unset default of the existing `native_tools` changes for `custom` aliases (documented in `docs/book/src/providers/custom.md` and the schema doc comment).
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- Exact upgrade steps for existing users: if your custom endpoint does not support native tool calling, add `native_tools = false` to its `[providers.models.custom.<alias>]` entry to skip the failing first request.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert` the default-flip commit; the streaming dedup commit is independent.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** `native_tools = false` on the alias restores the previous behavior without a revert.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** a `Native tool calling failed for custom provider alias ...` warning in the turn status or log for an endpoint that rejects native tools; provider errors mentioning `tools` or `tool_choice` for that alias.

prs.title: feat(zerocode): reopen open sessions when zerocode restarts
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - zerocode's sidebar list of open sessions lived only in memory. The daemon keeps every transcript, but quitting zerocode lost which sessions were open, so each launch started from an empty sidebar.
  - The list (session ids, agent aliases, order, focus, and the last Chat/Code pane on screen) is now saved whenever it changes, as an owner-only JSON file per connection target under `<config-dir>/open-sessions/`.
  - At launch the saved list goes to the existing reconnect resume path (`set_resume_sessions`), so restored sessions reattach by id exactly as they do after a daemon reconnect: focused first, the rest in the background.
  - On by default (`[sidebar] restore_sessions = true`). `zerocode --fresh` starts one launch with an empty sidebar and still saves its own list.
  - Over a local socket, saved sessions the daemon no longer lists (deleted or pruned) are dropped with one notice. Over WSS that check is skipped, because `session/list` there only returns sessions the current client instance owns, which after a restart is none. Remote entries go straight to resume, which already keeps a failed entry as a retryable row.
- **Scope boundary:** Client only (`apps/zerocode`); no daemon, RPC or runtime change. Queued messages, unsent drafts and attachments are not saved. A turn that was running when zerocode quit is not resumed or rerun.
- **Blast radius:** zerocode startup (one extra `session/list-acp` and/or `session/list` call on a local connection when a saved list exists) and the per-frame sidebar derivation (a cheap comparison; the file is written only when the list changes, and never while disconnected).
- **Linked issue(s):** None.

### What this does, simply

When you quit zerocode and start it again, the sessions you had open in the sidebar come back: same order, same one focused, on the pane you were using. The conversations themselves were always kept by the daemon. What was lost was the list of which ones you had open. If a saved session has since been deleted, it is skipped with a short notice. Use `zerocode --fresh` to start one launch with an empty sidebar, or set `restore_sessions = false` under `[sidebar]` to turn the feature off.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface` = `tui` (zerocode Chat and Code panes)
- **Setup / preconditions:** A local daemon with at least two agents.
- **Steps to run:** Open two Code sessions and one Chat session from the sidebar, focus the second Code session, quit zerocode, start it again. Then quit and start once more with `zerocode --fresh`.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The second launch opens on the Code pane with the same three sidebar rows in the same order and the second Code session focused, transcripts loaded. The `--fresh` launch starts with an empty sidebar.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** Every launch starts with an empty sidebar (or the recent-session picker); the previous launch's open sessions must be reopened one by one.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `Test` and `Lint` cover the zerocode crate.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** No end-to-end launch against a real daemon in CI; the unit tests drive the resume path with a mocked RPC transport.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
$ zc-cargo test -p zerocode            (remote, Mac mini, head 261cad73428e)
test open_sessions::tests::saved_list_round_trips_in_order_with_focus ... ok
test open_sessions::tests::each_connection_target_keeps_its_own_list ... ok
test open_sessions::tests::local_restore_asks_the_daemon_and_drops_what_it_lacks ... ok
test open_sessions::tests::remote_restore_keeps_the_list_without_asking ... ok
test chat::tests::saved_open_sessions_reattach_by_id_at_launch ... ok
test config::tests::restore_sessions_defaults_on_and_is_env_overridable ... ok
test app::tests::fresh_skips_restore_but_keeps_saving ... ok
test i18n::tests::restore_sessions_messages_format_in_all_builtin_catalogues ... ok
test result: FAILED. 1472 passed; 1 failed; 2 ignored
  (the one failure is connection_tests::insecure_tls_prompt_preserves_default_sigint,
   which fails the same way on master on that machine)

$ zc-cargo clippy -p zerocode --all-targets -- -D warnings
CLIPPY_EXIT=0

$ rustfmt --edition 2024 --check <changed files>   -> clean
$ bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh          -> Comment hygiene gate passed.
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** That the WSS guard is load-bearing: with it removed, `remote_restore_keeps_the_list_without_asking` fails. Not yet verified: a real launch against a live daemon (see below).
- **Visual interface evidence:** I'm verifying this in the experiment build.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `261cad73428e`, zerocode TUI, unit tests above.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A (verifying in the experiment build).
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** See the reviewer steps above.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Full workspace test; the change is confined to `apps/zerocode`.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? Yes: zerocode writes one new file per connection target under its own config directory. It is written owner-only (`0600`) and atomically, through the same `secure_file::write_private_atomic` funnel as `zerocode-config.toml`.
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No. The file holds session ids, agent aliases and the connection label (socket path or WSS URL). The label is already shown on the dashboard. Credentials are not stored.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: see the first item.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes. A config file without `restore_sessions` restores (default on); a missing, damaged or newer-format list file is ignored.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes: `[sidebar] restore_sessions` (env `ZEROCODE_sidebar__restore_sessions`) and the `--fresh` flag. Documented in `docs/book/src/zerocode/config.md`.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: nothing to do on upgrade. To keep the old behavior, set `restore_sessions = false` under `[sidebar]`.

prs.title: fix(channels): parse flat inbound Lark post content
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Feishu delivers inbound rich-text (`post`) messages with a flat body (`{"title":…,"content":[…]}`); `parse_post_content_details` only accepted the locale-wrapped body used when *sending* (`{"zh_cn":{…}}`), so every inbound `post` message was dropped before any reply.
  - A formatted list typed in the Feishu client *is* that flat `post` body — the `1. `/`- ` marker is plain text in the first element — so list messages looked silently ignored while plain `text` messages kept working.
  - Accept the flat body (plus the `content_v2` alias the same payload carries) in addition to the locale-wrapped shape, with a regression test built from a captured inbound payload.
- **Scope boundary:** the inbound `post` content decoder (`parse_post_content_details`), two regression tests, and the CI selector that runs the full Lark test module. Outbound post construction, the `list` message-type branch, group-mention policy, and every other channel are untouched.
- **Blast radius:** all Lark channel users sending rich text, in direct and group chats. The function is shared by the websocket listener and by `parse_event_payload` (HTTP/webhook ingress), so both paths change. Locale-wrapped payloads keep their existing precedence and behavior.
- **Linked issue(s):** None.

### What this does, simply

When you type a line into the Feishu (Lark) client that starts with a list marker such as `- ` or `1. `, the client does not send a `text` message. It sends a rich-text `post` message whose body is a flat JSON object, `{"title":"","content":[[…]],"content_v2":[[…]]}`, with the list marker as ordinary text inside the first element.

ZeroClaw's Lark decoder only understood the *sending* shape of a post, where the body is wrapped in a language key, `{"zh_cn":{"title":…,"content":[…]}}`. Fed the flat inbound body, none of its lookup branches matched, the function returned `None`, and the message was discarded before the agent was ever asked — no reply, no reaction, and not even an INFO trace line (the drop is logged at DEBUG level). Plain `text` messages never hit that path, which is why only rich text looked broken.

This PR teaches the decoder to accept the flat inbound body as well, and prefers `content` with `content_v2` as a fallback. Rich text, including lists, now reaches the agent like any other message. Posts with no extractable text remain ignored; untitled posts with text are accepted. Nothing about how ZeroClaw *sends* rich text changed.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `Yes` — the fix is about the shape of a live inbound event, so live A/B is the most direct demonstration.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `channel: lark`
- **Setup / preconditions:** a Lark channel configured and reachable from a Feishu client (bot present in the chat).
- **Steps to run:** in the chat with the bot, send one line starting with `- ` or `1. ` (the client converts it into a rich-text/list message).
- **Expected on this branch (after):** the runtime trace shows `channel inbound` carrying the parsed text, followed by a model turn and `channel outbound` / `reply delivered`; the chat receives an answer.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** running the same step produces no reply and no `channel inbound` event at all — the message is dropped during decode.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the workspace Rust gates exercise the changed function through `zeroclaw-channels`; the added unit test is the focused gate for this behavior.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** none that CI would miss. For reviewers running the local `.githooks/pre-push` hook on macOS: its final full-workspace `cargo test` step fails on the unrelated, pre-existing `zeroclaw-config::policy::tests::unix_foreign_null_spellings_get_no_filesystem_exception`, which creates the symlinks `nul` and `NUL` in one directory while the default APFS volume is case-insensitive (the second `symlink` returns `EEXIST`). The `rust_quality_gate` (fmt + clippy, whole workspace) and firmware protocol stages of the same hook pass on this branch.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```sh
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
# (no output)

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-channels --features channel-lark --all-targets -- -D warnings
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 1m 14s

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --features channel-lark --lib lark_parse_post
test lark::tests::lark_parse_post_message_accepts_md_tag_text_content ... ok
test lark::tests::lark_parse_post_message_accepts_flat_inbound_content ... FAILED

# before the fix, with the captured inbound payload:
#   assertion `left == right` failed
#     left: 0
#    right: 1

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --features channel-lark --lib lark::
test result: ok. 125 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 1975 filtered out
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** A live end-to-end run on a Lark-configured daemon: a formatted list message sent from the Feishu client produced `channel inbound` with the parsed text, a normal agent turn, and a delivered reply; the regression test uses the captured payload byte-for-byte. I did **not** verify group-chat rich text with an @-mention beyond the existing `lark_parse_post_message_preserves_at_mention_for_group_reply` test, and I did not test other message types.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `N/A` — message decoding only; no layout, styling, or interaction change.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `channel: lark`, exercised live against a locally built daemon.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** sent a list-formatted rich-text message → agent turn ran → reply delivered to the chat.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** `N/A`

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? (`No`)
- New external network calls? (`No`)
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? (`No`)
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, or docs? (`No`)
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? (`Yes`) — previously dropped post text now reaches the existing inbound path. Sender authorization and group-mention filtering remain in place, with the same trust boundary as other channel text.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: `N/A`

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? (`Yes`)
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? (`No`)
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? (`No`)
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: `N/A`
